exercises.title: Your First HTML Page
exercises.description: Create a basic HTML page with the required document structure.
exercises.instructions:
Every HTML page needs a basic structure to work properly. Create a valid HTML5 page by adding the required elements.

Your page should have:
- A `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the very top
- An `<html>` element with `lang="en"`
- A `<head>` section
- A `<body>` section

This is the skeleton that every web page is built on.

<!-- Add the DOCTYPE declaration -->

<!-- Add the html element with lang="en" -->

  <!-- Add the head section -->

  <!-- Add the body section -->
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: Every HTML page starts with a special declaration that tells the browser what version of HTML you are using. What does that declaration look like?
The structure is: DOCTYPE at the top, then an <html> element that contains both a <head> and a <body> section.

exercises.title: Page Title
exercises.description: Add a title to your HTML page that appears in the browser tab.
exercises.instructions:
The `<title>` element sets the text that appears in the browser tab. It must be placed inside the `<head>` section.

Add a `<title>` element inside the `<head>` with the text "My First Page".

Example: When you open a website, the text you see on the browser tab is the page title.
exercises.starterCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <!-- Add a title element with the text "My First Page" -->

  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
hints: There is a specific HTML element that controls what text appears in the browser tab. Where should it be placed — in the head or the body?
The <title> element goes inside the <head> section. The text you want displayed goes between the opening and closing title tags.

exercises.title: Head and Body
exercises.description: Add a title in the head and a heading in the body of an HTML page.
exercises.instructions:
The `<head>` contains information about the page (like the title). The `<body>` contains what visitors actually see.

Add:
- A `<title>` element inside `<head>` with the text "Hello World"
- An `<h1>` element inside `<body>` with the text "Welcome!"

Remember: The head is for the browser, the body is for the viewer.

  <body>
    <!-- Add an h1 heading with "Welcome!" -->

  </body>
</html>
exercises.solution: Welcome!
hints: The page has two main sections. One holds information the browser uses behind the scenes, and the other holds content the visitor sees on screen.
Use <title> inside <head> for the tab text. Use <h1> inside <body> for the visible heading.

exercises.title: Heading Levels
exercises.description: Use heading elements h1 through h3 to create a content hierarchy.
exercises.instructions:
HTML has six levels of headings, from `<h1>` (most important) to `<h6>` (least important). They create a visual and structural hierarchy for your content.

Add the following headings in order:
- An `<h1>` with "Main Title"
- An `<h2>` with "Section Title"
- An `<h3>` with "Subsection Title"

Every page should have exactly one `<h1>`. Use `<h2>` through `<h6>` for subsections.

Use <h1> for the most important heading, <h2> for the next level, and <h3> for the level after that. Each has an opening and closing tag.

exercises.description: Use strong and em elements to add emphasis to text.
exercises.instructions:
HTML provides elements to add emphasis to text:
- `<strong>` makes text **bold** — use it for important content
- `<em>` makes text *italic* — use it for stressed emphasis

Create a paragraph that contains:
- The word "important" wrapped in `<strong>` tags
- The word "really" wrapped in `<em>` tags

The full text should read: "This is really important information."

hints: There are two HTML elements that change how text looks and what it means to screen readers. One makes text bold, the other italic.

exercises.title: Unordered List
exercises.description: Create a bulleted list using ul and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An unordered list displays items with bullet points. It uses two elements:
- `<ul>` — the list container (unordered list)
- `<li>` — each item in the list (list item)

Create an unordered list with three items:
- "Apples"
- "Bananas"
- "Oranges"

Every `<li>` must be inside a `<ul>` to work correctly.
exercises.solution:
• Apples
  • Bananas
  • Oranges
hints: An unordered list needs a container element and individual item elements inside it. What are the HTML tags for these?
The container is <ul> (unordered list). Each item uses <li> (list item) with the text between opening and closing tags.

exercises.title: Ordered List
exercises.description: Create a numbered list using ol and li elements.
exercises.instructions:
An ordered list displays items with numbers. It uses `<ol>` instead of `<ul>`, but the items still use `<li>`.

Create an ordered list with three steps:
1. "Preheat the oven"
2. "Mix the ingredients"
3. "Bake for 30 minutes"

The browser automatically numbers each item for you.
exercises.solution:
1. Preheat the oven
  2. Mix the ingredients
  3. Bake for 30 minutes
hints: A numbered list works just like a bulleted list, but uses a different container element. What tag creates a numbered (ordered) list?
Change <ul> to <ol> for ordered lists. The <li> elements stay the same — the browser handles the numbering automatically.

Use <h2> for the heading. Then create a <ul> with five or more <li> elements, each containing a grocery item.

exercises.title: Simple Table
exercises.description: Create a basic 2-column table with 3 rows of data.
exercises.instructions:
Tables use three main elements:
- `<table>` — the table container
- `<tr>` — a table row
- `<td>` — a table data cell

Create a table with 3 rows and 2 columns:
- Row 1: "Name" and "Age"
- Row 2: "Alex" and "25"
- Row 3: "Sam" and "30"

Each `<td>` goes inside a `<tr>`, and all `<tr>` elements go inside `<table>`.

Name Age
Alex 25
Sam 30

Use <tr> for each row and <td> for each cell within that row. Nest them inside a <table> element.

exercises.description: Use th elements to create bold header cells in a table.

Create a table with:
- A header row using `<th>` with "Product" and "Price"
- Two data rows using `<td>`:

  - "Tea" and "$2.50"

Tea $2.50

Product Price

Tea $2.50

Replace <td> with <th> for the first row to create header cells. Data rows still use <td>.

exercises.title: Table Sections
exercises.description: Organize a table into head, body, and foot sections.
exercises.instructions:

- `<thead>` — the header section (column labels)
- `<tbody>` — the body section (data rows)
- `<tfoot>` — the footer section (summary row)

Create a table with:
- `<thead>` containing a row with `<th>` cells: "Item" and "Cost"
- `<tbody>` containing two rows: "Lunch" / "$12" and "Dinner" / "$25"
- `<tfoot>` containing a row: "Total" and "$37"

Item Cost

Wrap your header row in <thead>, your data rows in <tbody>, and your summary row in <tfoot>. Each section still uses <tr> and <td>/<th> inside.

exercises.title: Relative Positioning
exercises.description: Nudge an element from its normal position using position relative.
exercises.instructions:
The `position: relative` property lets you move an element from where it would normally appear. Use `top`, `right`, `bottom`, or `left` to offset it.

Style the `.nudged` element:
- Set `position` to `relative`
- Set `top` to `20px` (pushes it down 20px from its normal position)
- Set `left` to `10px` (pushes it right 10px from its normal position)

The element still takes up its original space in the layout — it just renders shifted.

exercises.title: Absolute Positioning
exercises.description: Position an element precisely within a relative parent.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: absolute` is removed from the normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (a parent with `position: relative`).

The HTML has a `.container` (already set to `position: relative`) and a `.badge` inside it.

Style the `.badge` element:
- Set `position` to `absolute`
- Set `top` to `0`
- Set `right` to `0`

This pins the badge to the top-right corner of the container.

exercises.title: Fixed Header
exercises.description: Create a header that stays fixed at the top of the viewport.
exercises.instructions:
An element with `position: fixed` stays in the same position on screen even when the user scrolls. This is commonly used for navigation bars.

Style the `.header` element:

- Set `left` to `0`

exercises.title: Enable Flexbox
exercises.description: Apply display flex to a container to enable flexbox layout.
exercises.instructions:
Flexbox is a layout system that arranges items in a row or column. To use it, set `display: flex` on the container element.

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`

Once flexbox is enabled, its children automatically arrange in a horizontal row. Without flexbox, block elements stack vertically.

exercises.title: Flex Direction
exercises.description: Arrange flex items in a row or column using flex-direction.

The `flex-direction` property controls whether flex items arrange horizontally (`row`) or vertically (`column`).

Style the `.container` element:

- Set `flex-direction` to `column`

Top

exercises.title: Justify Content
exercises.description: Distribute flex items along the main axis using justify-content.
exercises.instructions:
The `justify-content` property controls how items are distributed along the main axis (horizontally in a row, vertically in a column).

Style the `.container` element:
- Set `display` to `flex`
- Set `justify-content` to `space-between`

Common values: `flex-start`, `flex-end`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.

`space-between` puts equal space between items, with the first and last items flush against the edges.

Left
Center
Right

exercises.title: Align Items
exercises.description: Align flex items along the cross axis using align-items.

The `align-items` property controls how items are aligned along the cross axis (vertical in a row, horizontal in a column).

Style the `.container` element:

Short

Short

exercises.title: Gap
exercises.description: Add space between flex items using the gap property.

The `gap` property adds space between flex items without needing margins. It only creates space between items, not around the outer edges.

Style the `.container` element:

Style the `.grid` element:

exercises.description: Use grid-template-columns with different widths to create varied columns.

exercises.title: Viewport Meta
exercises.description: Add the viewport meta tag to make a page mobile-friendly.
exercises.instructions:
Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render pages at a desktop width and then zoom out, making text tiny. The viewport meta tag tells the browser to match the device width.

Add a `<meta>` tag inside `<head>` with:
- `name` set to `"viewport"`
- `content` set to `"width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"`

This single tag is the foundation of responsive web design. Every modern web page should include it.

Mobile-Friendly Page

exercises.title: Fluid Widths
exercises.description: Use percentages and max-width for fluid, responsive sizing.
exercises.instructions:
Fixed pixel widths break on smaller screens. Using percentages with `max-width` creates fluid layouts that adapt to any screen size.

Style the `.content` element:
- Set `width` to `100%`
- Set `max-width` to `600px`
- Set `margin` to `0 auto` (to center it)

Responsive Content

exercises.title: Define a Custom Property
exercises.description: Create a CSS custom property on the root element.
exercises.instructions:
CSS custom properties (also called CSS variables) let you store values and reuse them throughout your stylesheet. They always start with two dashes (`--`).

Define a custom property on `:root`:
- `--primary-color` with the value `#3b82f6`

Then style the `.box` element:
- Set `background-color` to use the custom property with `var(--primary-color)`

The `:root` selector targets the document root, making the variable available everywhere.

exercises.title: Use Multiple Variables
exercises.description: Apply multiple CSS custom properties to style an element.
exercises.instructions:
Custom properties shine when you define a set of related values and reuse them across your styles.

- `--bg-dark` with value `#1e293b`
- `--text-light` with value `#f1f5f9`

Then style the `.card` element:
- Set `background-color` using `var(--bg-dark)`
- Set `color` using `var(--text-light)`

This pattern is the foundation of CSS theming.

Dark Card

exercises.title: Box Shadow
exercises.description: Add a shadow effect to an element using box-shadow.
exercises.instructions:
The `box-shadow` property adds a shadow effect around an element's frame. The values are: `x-offset y-offset blur-radius color`.

Style the `.card` element:

Shadows add depth and make elements feel like they float above the page.

Card Title

The `text-shadow` property adds a shadow behind text characters. The values are the same as box-shadow: `x-offset y-offset blur-radius color`.

Style the `h1` element:

exercises.title: Arrow Functions
exercises.description: Write a function using arrow function syntax.
exercises.instructions:
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write functions. Instead of the `function` keyword, you use `=>` (an arrow).

Regular: `function double(n) { return n * 2; }`
Arrow: `const double = (n) => { return n * 2; };`

Write an arrow function called `triple` that takes a number `n` and returns `n * 3`.

Example: `triple(4)` should return `12`
Example: `triple(0)` should return `0`
hints: Arrow functions are stored in a variable using `const`. The arrow `=>` replaces the `function` keyword.
Inside the curly braces, use `return n * 3;` just like in a regular function.

exercises.title: Block Scope
exercises.description: Demonstrate how let variables are scoped to their block.
exercises.instructions:
Variables declared with `let` and `const` only exist inside the block `{ }` where they are declared. This is called block scope.

Write a function called `scopeTest` that:
1. Declares `let message = "outside"` before the if block
2. Inside an `if (true)` block, declares `let message = "inside"` (this is a separate variable!)
3. Returns the outer `message` variable after the if block

Because `let` is block-scoped, the inner `message` does not affect the outer one. The function should return `"outside"`.
hints: When you declare a variable with `let` inside a block (like an `if` statement), it is completely separate from any variable with the same name outside that block.
Declare `let message = "outside";` before the `if`. Inside the `if`, declare `let message = "inside";`. After the `if`, return `message` — it will be the outer one.

exercises.title: ForEach
exercises.description: Use forEach to perform an action on each element in an array.
exercises.instructions:
The `.forEach()` method calls a function once for each element in an array. It is a cleaner alternative to a `for` loop when you need to do something with every item.

Write a function called `addExcitement` that takes an array of strings `words` and returns a new array where each string has `"!"` added to the end.

Use `.forEach()` to loop through the array and build the result.

Example: `addExcitement(["hi", "bye"])` should return `["hi!", "bye!"]`
hints: Start by creating an empty array to store results. Then use `.forEach()` to visit each element and add it (with modifications) to the result array.
Declare `const result = [];` before the loop. Inside forEach, use `result.push(word + "!");` to add each modified word.

exercises.title: Map — Double
exercises.description: Use the map method to transform every element in an array.
exercises.instructions:
The `.map()` method creates a new array by calling a function on every element. The original array is not changed.

Write a function called `doubleAll` that takes an array of numbers `nums` and returns a new array where every number is doubled.

Use `.map()` instead of a loop.

Example: `doubleAll([1, 2, 3])` should return `[2, 4, 6]`
Example: `doubleAll([0, -5])` should return `[0, -10]`
hints: The `.map()` method takes a function that receives each element one at a time. Whatever that function returns becomes the new element in the output array.
Call `nums.map(function(num) { return num * 2; })` to double each element. Return the result of `.map()` directly.

exercises.title: Filter — Evens
exercises.description: Use the filter method to keep only elements that match a condition.
exercises.instructions:
The `.filter()` method creates a new array containing only the elements where a test function returns `true`. Elements that return `false` are left out.

Write a function called `getEvens` that takes an array of numbers `nums` and returns a new array containing only the even numbers.

A number is even if `num % 2 === 0` (the remainder when divided by 2 is 0).

Example: `getEvens([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])` should return `[2, 4, 6]`
Example: `getEvens([1, 3, 5])` should return `[]`
hints: The `.filter()` method takes a function that returns `true` to keep an element or `false` to skip it. The modulo operator `%` gives you the remainder after division.
Call `nums.filter(function(num) { return num % 2 === 0; })` — if the remainder is 0, the number is even and gets kept.

exercises.title: Object with Method
exercises.description: Add a method to an object that returns a formatted string.
exercises.instructions:
A method is a function stored as an object property. Inside a method, `this` refers to the object the method belongs to.

Write a function called `createDog` that returns an object with:
- A `name` property set to `"Rex"`
- A `breed` property set to `"Labrador"`
- A `describe` method that returns `"Rex is a Labrador"` (using `this.name` and `this.breed`)

Example: `createDog().describe()` should return `"Rex is a Labrador"`
hints: A method is a property whose value is a function. Inside that function, `this` refers to the object itself, so you can access other properties.
Add `describe: function() { return this.name + " is a " + this.breed; }` as a property in the object.

exercises.title: Bracket Notation
exercises.description: Access object properties using a variable with bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
Bracket notation lets you access a property using a variable or string: `object[variableName]` or `object["propertyName"]`.

This is useful when the property name is stored in a variable.

Write a function called `getProperty` that takes an object `obj` and a string `key`, and returns the value of that property.

Example: `getProperty({ name: "Alice", age: 25 }, "name")` should return `"Alice"`
Example: `getProperty({ name: "Alice", age: 25 }, "age")` should return `25`
hints: When the property name is stored in a variable, you cannot use dot notation. You need a different notation that uses square brackets.
Use `obj[key]` — the variable `key` holds the property name as a string, and bracket notation looks it up.

exercises.title: Object.keys
exercises.description: Get all property names from an object as an array.
exercises.instructions:
`Object.keys(obj)` returns an array of all the property names (keys) in an object.

Write a function called `getKeys` that takes an object `obj` and returns an array of its keys.

Example: `getKeys({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 })` should return `["a", "b", "c"]`
hints: JavaScript has a built-in method on the `Object` class that extracts all property names from an object and returns them as an array.
Call `Object.keys(obj)` and return the result. It gives you an array like `["a", "b", "c"]`.

exercises.title: Object.values
exercises.description: Get all property values from an object as an array.
exercises.instructions:
`Object.values(obj)` returns an array of all the values in an object (without the keys).

Write a function called `getValues` that takes an object `obj` and returns an array of its values.

Example: `getValues({ a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 })` should return `[1, 2, 3]`
hints: Just like `Object.keys()` returns the names, there is a similar method that returns only the values.
Call `Object.values(obj)` to get an array of all the values in the object.

exercises.title: Access Nested Property
exercises.description: Access a property inside a nested object.
exercises.instructions:
Objects can contain other objects. To access deeply nested properties, chain dot notation: `obj.outer.inner`.

Write a function called `getCityName` that takes an object `user` with this structure:
```
{ name: "Alice", address: { city: "Seattle", state: "WA" } }
```
and returns the value of the `city` property.

Example: `getCityName({ name: "Alice", address: { city: "Seattle", state: "WA" } })` should return `"Seattle"`
hints: When an object is nested inside another object, you can chain dots to go deeper level by level.
First access `user.address` to get the inner object, then `.city` to get the city: `user.address.city`.

exercises.title: Object Destructuring
exercises.description: Extract properties from an object into individual variables.
exercises.instructions:
Destructuring lets you unpack properties from an object into separate variables in one step:

```
const { name, age } = person;
```

This creates two variables, `name` and `age`, with values from the object.

Write a function called `introduce` that takes an object with `name` and `age` properties. Use destructuring to extract them, then return `"I am name and I am age years old"`.

Example: `introduce({ name: "Alice", age: 25 })` should return `"I am Alice and I am 25 years old"`
hints: Destructuring uses curly braces on the left side of an assignment. The variable names must match the property names in the object.
Write `const { name, age } = person;` to create two variables. Then use them in the return string.

exercises.title: Array Destructuring
exercises.description: Extract elements from an array into individual variables.
exercises.instructions:
Array destructuring works like object destructuring, but uses square brackets and assigns by position:

```
const [first, second] = myArray;

Write `const [first, second] = arr;` to extract the first two elements, then return them combined with " and ".

exercises.title: Multiple Methods
exercises.description: Add multiple methods to a class that modify and read its state.

Classes can have multiple methods that work together to manage the object's data.

```

exercises.title: Change Text

exercises.title: Create Element
exercises.description: Create a new element and add it to the page.
exercises.instructions:
To add new content to a page, you: 1. Create an element with `document.createElement("tag")` 2. Set its content with `.textContent` 3. Add it to the page with `parent.appendChild(element)` Write a function called `addParagraph` that creates a new `

` element with the text `"New paragraph"` and appends it to the `document.body`. The page starts empty. After calling `addParagraph()`, it should have one `

` element.
hints: Creating an element is a two-step process: first you make the element, then you place it somewhere on the page.
Use `document.createElement("p")` to make the element. Set `.textContent` to add text. Then call `document.body.appendChild()` to add it to the page.

exercises.title: Click Handler
exercises.description: Add a click event listener that changes an element's text.
exercises.instructions:
The `addEventListener` method attaches a function to an event on an element. When the event happens, the function runs.

Write a function called `setupClick` that:
1. Selects the button with id `"btn"`
2. Adds a `"click"` event listener
3. When clicked, the button's text should change to `"Clicked!"`

The page has this HTML:
```html
<button id="btn">Click me</button>
```
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Set up the button with id "btn" so that clicking it
 * changes its text to "Clicked!".
 *
 * Page HTML: <button id="btn">Click me</button>
 *
 * Write a function called setupClick that wires up the event.
 */

// Write your code below
hints: Use `addEventListener` with two arguments: the event name (a string like `"click"`) and a function that should run when the event happens.
Select the button, then call `.addEventListener("click", function() { ... });`. Inside the function, change the button's `textContent`.

exercises.title: Button Counter
exercises.description: Count button clicks and display the running total.
exercises.instructions: Build a click counter that tracks how many times a button has been clicked and displays the count. Write a function called `setupCounter` that: 1. Selects the button with id `"counter-btn"` 2. Selects the span with id `"count"` 3. Keeps a running count starting at `0` 4. Each click increases the count by 1 and updates the span's text The page has this HTML: ```html 0 ```
exercises.starterCode: /** * Set up a click counter: each click on the button increments * a count and updates the display. * * Page HTML: * * 0 * * Write a function called setupCounter that wires everything up. */ // Write your code below
hints: Declare a variable outside the event listener to keep track of the count. Inside the listener, increment it and update the display.
Declare `let count = 0;` before the listener. In the click handler, write `count = count + 1;` then `display.textContent = count;`.

exercises.title: Styled Heading
exercises.description: Create and style a page title with a custom font color and size.
exercises.instructions:
Create an `<h1>` element with the text `"Welcome"` and style it with CSS.

**HTML requirements:**
- An `<h1>` element containing `"Welcome"`

**CSS requirements:**
- Set the `h1` color to `#1e40af` (a blue)
- Set the `h1` font-size to `36px`
- Center the text with `text-align: center`
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Add your h1 element -->
exercises.solution: Welcome
hints: Write the HTML element first, then add CSS rules targeting that element. Use the `h1` selector in CSS.
In the CSS panel, write `h1 { color: #1e40af; font-size: 36px; text-align: center; }` to apply all three styles.

exercises.title: Styled List
exercises.description: Build a bulleted list and style it with custom spacing and color.
exercises.instructions:
Create an unordered list with three items and style it.

**HTML requirements:**
- A `<ul>` element
- Three `<li>` elements with the text: `"HTML"`, `"CSS"`, `"JavaScript"`

**CSS requirements:**
- Set `li` color to `#047857` (green)
- Set `li` padding to `8px`
- Set `li` font-size to `18px`
exercises.starterCode: <!-- Add your list here -->
exercises.solution:
• HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript
hints: Write the HTML list structure first with `<ul>` and `<li>` tags, then add CSS rules targeting the `li` selector.
In CSS, write `li { color: #047857; padding: 8px; font-size: 18px; }` to style all list items.

exercises.instructions:
Build a simple card component using a `

` with the class `card` - Inside it, an `

exercises.title: Centered Content
exercises.description: Center a content block on the page using margin auto.
exercises.instructions:
Create a content container and center it horizontally on the page. **HTML requirements:** - A `
` with the class `container` - Inside it, an `

` with text `"Centered Page"` - A `

` with any text you choose **CSS requirements:** - `.container` max-width: `600px` - `.container` margin-left and margin-right: `auto` (centers the block) - `.container` padding: `20px`

Centered Page

In CSS, write `.container { max-width: 600px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 20px; }` — the `auto` margins center it.

exercises.title: Styled Input
exercises.description: Style a text input with custom border, padding, and font size.
exercises.instructions:
Create a labeled text input and style it.

**HTML requirements:**
- A `<label>` with the text `"Name:"`
- An `<input>` with `type="text"` and `id="name-input"`

**CSS requirements:**
- `input` padding: `10px`
- `input` font-size: `16px`
- `input` border: `2px solid #6366f1` (indigo)

<label>Name:</label>
<input type="text" id="name-input">

In CSS: `input { padding: 10px; font-size: 16px; border: 2px solid #6366f1; border-radius: 4px; }`.

exercises.title: Spread Array
exercises.description: Copy and merge arrays using the spread operator.
exercises.instructions:
The spread operator `...` expands an array into individual elements. It can be used to copy arrays or combine them.

Copy: `const copy = [...original];`
Merge: `const merged = [...arr1, ...arr2];`

Write a function called `mergeArrays` that takes two arrays `a` and `b` and returns a new array containing all elements from both, with `a`'s elements first.

Example: `mergeArrays([1, 2], [3, 4])` should return `[1, 2, 3, 4]`
hints: The spread operator `...` takes all the elements out of an array. Inside new square brackets, you can spread multiple arrays together.
Write `return [...a, ...b];` to create a new array with all elements from `a` followed by all elements from `b`.

exercises.title: Spread Object
exercises.description: Copy and extend objects using the spread operator.
exercises.instructions:
The spread operator also works with objects. You can copy all properties from one object into a new one, and add or override properties.

Copy: `const copy = { ...original };`
Extend: `const extended = { ...original, newProp: value };`

Write a function called `addEmail` that takes an object `person` and a string `email`, and returns a new object with all of the person's properties plus an `email` property.

Example: `addEmail({ name: "Alice" }, "alice@test.com")` should return `{ name: "Alice", email: "alice@test.com" }`
hints: The spread operator works with objects too — `...person` inside curly braces copies all of that object's properties into a new object.
Write `return { ...person, email: email };` to create a new object with everything from `person` plus the email.

exercises.title: Try/Catch
exercises.description: Wrap risky code in try/catch and handle the error gracefully.
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Parses a JSON string safely. Returns the parsed value on success,
 * or "Invalid JSON" if parsing fails.
 *
 * Example: safeParse('{"a":1}') → { a: 1 }
 * Example: safeParse("not json") → "Invalid JSON"
 * Example: safeParse('"hello"') → "hello"
 */
hints: Put the code that might fail inside the `try` block. If an error happens, the `catch` block runs instead of crashing.
In the `try`, write `return JSON.parse(jsonStr);`. In the `catch`, write `return "Invalid JSON";`.

exercises.title: Status Codes
exercises.description: Write a function that returns the meaning of common HTTP status codes.
exercises.instructions:
HTTP status codes tell the client what happened with their request. Common codes include:
- `200`: OK (success)
- `201`: Created (new resource made)
- `404`: Not Found (resource doesn't exist)
- `500`: Internal Server Error (something went wrong on the server)

Write a function called `getStatusMessage` that takes a number `code` and returns the matching message string.

Example: `getStatusMessage(200)` should return `"OK"`
Example: `getStatusMessage(404)` should return `"Not Found"`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Given an HTTP status code, return its meaning.
 * 200 → "OK", 201 → "Created", 404 → "Not Found",
 * 500 → "Internal Server Error", anything else → "Unknown"
 *
 * Example: getStatusMessage(200) → "OK"
 * Example: getStatusMessage(999) → "Unknown"
 */
hints: You can use a series of `if` statements or a `switch` to check the code and return the matching message.
Check each code with `if (code === 200) return "OK";` and so on. Add a final `return "Unknown";` for any unrecognized code.

exercises.title: HTTP Methods
exercises.description: Identify which HTTP method matches each CRUD operation.
exercises.instructions:
HTTP methods tell the server what action to perform. The four main methods map to CRUD operations:
- **C**reate → `POST`
- **R**ead → `GET`
- **U**pdate → `PUT`
- **D**elete → `DELETE`

Write a function called `getHttpMethod` that takes a CRUD operation string and returns the matching HTTP method.

Example: `getHttpMethod("create")` should return `"POST"`
Example: `getHttpMethod("read")` should return `"GET"`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Given a CRUD operation string, return the matching HTTP method.
 * "create" → "POST", "read" → "GET",
 * "update" → "PUT", "delete" → "DELETE"
 *
 * Example: getHttpMethod("create") → "POST"
 * Example: getHttpMethod("read") → "GET"
 */
hints: There are four standard HTTP methods that correspond to the four CRUD operations. Each operation has exactly one matching method.
Use `if` statements: `if (operation === "create") return "POST";` and continue for read/GET, update/PUT, delete/DELETE.

exercises.title: Request Object
exercises.description: Create an object representing an HTTP request.
exercises.instructions:
An HTTP request has several parts: the method (GET, POST, etc.), the path (URL), and optionally a body (data being sent).

Write a function called `createRequest` that takes `method`, `path`, and `body` parameters and returns an object with those three properties.

Example: `createRequest("GET", "/users", null)` should return `{ method: "GET", path: "/users", body: null }`
hints: An object literal with matching property names can be returned directly from the function.
Write `return { method: method, path: path, body: body };` to create the request object.

exercises.title: Simple Router
exercises.description: Match a URL path to a handler function and return the result.
exercises.instructions:
A router matches URL paths to the right piece of code (handler). This is how servers know what to do with each request.

Write a function called `route` that takes a `path` string and returns:
- `"Home Page"` for `"/"`
- `"About Page"` for `"/about"`
- `"Contact Page"` for `"/contact"`
- `"Not Found"` for anything else

Example: `route("/")` should return `"Home Page"`
Example: `route("/about")` should return `"About Page"`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Match a URL path to a page name.
 * "/" → "Home Page", "/about" → "About Page",
 * "/contact" → "Contact Page", anything else → "Not Found"
 *
 * Example: route("/") → "Home Page"
 * Example: route("/xyz") → "Not Found"
 */
hints: A router is just conditional logic — check the path against known values and return the matching response.
Use `if (path === "/") return "Home Page";` for each route. End with `return "Not Found";` as the default.

exercises.title: CRUD Functions
exercises.description: Write create, read, update, and delete functions for an in-memory list.
exercises.instructions:
CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic data operations.

Write four functions that manage an array called `items` (already declared for you):
- `addItem(item)` — pushes the item to the array and returns the array
- `getItems()` — returns the entire array
- `updateItem(index, newValue)` — replaces the item at the given index and returns the array
- `removeItem(index)` — removes the item at the given index using splice and returns the array

Example: After `addItem("apple")` and `addItem("banana")`, `getItems()` returns `["apple", "banana"]`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Build four functions that manage an in-memory array of items:
 *
 * addItem(item) — pushes item to the array, returns the array
 * getItems() — returns the array
 * updateItem(index, newValue) — replaces item at index, returns the array
 * removeItem(index) — removes item at index, returns the array
 *
 * The array should be declared outside the functions so all four share it.
 */
hints: Each function performs one operation on the shared `items` array. `push` adds to the end, bracket assignment updates, and `splice` removes.
For `addItem`: `items.push(item)`. For `updateItem`: `items[index] = newValue`. For `removeItem`: `items.splice(index, 1)`.

exercises.title: Define a Schema
exercises.description: Create an object describing the required fields and their types for a data model.
exercises.instructions:
A schema defines what shape your data should have — which fields are required and what types they should be.

Write a function called `getUserSchema` that returns an object describing a user's data shape:
- `name`: `"string"`
- `age`: `"number"`
- `email`: `"string"`
- `isActive`: `"boolean"`

Example: `getUserSchema().name` should return `"string"`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Return an object representing a user schema where keys are
 * field names and values are expected type strings.
 *
 * Fields: name (string), age (number), email (string), isActive (boolean)
 *
 * Example: getUserSchema().name → "string"
 * Example: getUserSchema().isActive → "boolean"
 */
hints: A schema is just a plain object where the keys are field names and the values describe what type each field should be.
Return `{ name: "string", age: "number", email: "string", isActive: "boolean" }`.

exercises.title: Validate Types
exercises.description: Check if a data object's fields match the expected types from a schema.
exercises.instructions:
After defining a schema, you need to validate that real data matches it.

Write a function called `validateTypes` that takes a `data` object and a `schema` object. It should return `true` if every field in the schema exists in the data AND has the correct type, or `false` otherwise.

Use `typeof` to check each field's type.

Example:
```
const schema = { name: "string", age: "number" };
validateTypes({ name: "Alice", age: 25 }, schema) // true
validateTypes({ name: "Alice", age: "25" }, schema) // false (age is string)
```
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Check if every field in a data object matches the types
 * defined in a schema object. Return true if all match, false otherwise.
 *
 * Example: validateTypes({ name: "Alice", age: 25 }, { name: "string", age: "number" }) → true
 * Example: validateTypes({ name: "Alice", age: "25" }, { name: "string", age: "number" }) → false
 */
hints: Loop through the schema keys and compare `typeof data[key]` with the expected type string in `schema[key]`.
If `typeof data[key] !== schema[key]`, return `false` immediately. If you finish the loop without returning false, return `true`.

exercises.title: Render a Greeting
exercises.description: Write a function that returns an element description object.
exercises.instructions:
In modern web frameworks, components are functions that return descriptions of what to display. Instead of directly creating DOM elements, they return plain objects. Write a function called `Greeting` that returns an object with: - `tag`: `"h1"` - `text`: `"Hello, World!"` This represents an `

Hello, World!

` element. Example: `Greeting()` should return `{ tag: "h1", text: "Hello, World!" }`
hints: A component is just a function that returns an object. The object describes what should appear on the page.
Return `{ tag: "h1", text: "Hello, World!" }` from the function.

exercises.title: Parameterized Render
exercises.description: Write a component function that accepts data and returns a customized element.
exercises.instructions:
Real components accept data (called "props" in frameworks) and use it to customize their output.

Write a function called `UserCard` that takes a `name` parameter and returns an object with:
- `tag`: `"div"`
- `text`: `"Welcome, "` followed by the name

Example: `UserCard("Alice")` should return `{ tag: "div", text: "Welcome, Alice" }`
hints: The function takes a parameter and uses it to build the text property of the returned object.
Return `{ tag: "div", text: "Welcome, " + name }` to combine the greeting with the parameter.

exercises.title: Props Object
exercises.description: Write a component function that reads data from a props object.
exercises.instructions:
Instead of passing individual parameters, frameworks pass a single "props" object containing all the data a component needs.

Write a function called `ProfileCard` that takes a `props` object with `name` and `role` properties, and returns an object with:
- `tag`: `"div"`
- `text`: the name followed by ` - ` followed by the role

Example: `ProfileCard({ name: "Alice", role: "Developer" })` should return `{ tag: "div", text: "Alice - Developer" }`
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Given a props object with name and role properties, return an
 * element description with tag "div" and text "name - role".
 *
 * Example: ProfileCard({ name: "Alice", role: "Developer" })
 *   → { tag: "div", text: "Alice - Developer" }
 */
hints: The `props` parameter is a regular object. Access its properties with dot notation like `props.name` and `props.role`.
Return `{ tag: "div", text: props.name + " - " + props.role }` to build the text from props.

exercises.title: State Object
exercises.description: Create an initial state object and return a fresh copy each time.
exercises.instructions:
State represents the current data in your application. To avoid bugs, you should always work with copies of state rather than modifying the original directly.

Write a function called `getInitialState` that returns a NEW object each time it is called, with:
- `count`: `0`
- `items`: `[]` (empty array)
- `isLoading`: `false`

Important: Each call should return a brand new object, not the same one.

Example: `getInitialState().count` should return `0`
Example: `getInitialState() !== getInitialState()` should be `true` (different objects)
exercises.starterCode:
/**
 * Return a fresh state object each time with:
 * - count: 0
 * - items: [] (empty array)
 * - isLoading: false
 *
 * Each call must return a NEW object (not the same reference).
 * Example: getInitialState().count → 0
 */
hints: If you create the object inside the function using a literal `{ }`, a new object is created each time the function is called.
Just return `{ count: 0, items: [], isLoading: false }` directly — since it is inside the function, it creates a fresh object each call.

exercises.title: Declare with Let
exercises.description: Declare five variables using the let keyword.
exercises.instructions:
The `let` keyword creates a variable that can be reassigned later. Use `let` when you expect the value might change.

Declare these five variables using `let`:
1. `message` with the value `"Hello, world!"`
2. `year` with the value `2026`
3. `isOnline` with the value `true`
4. `activeUsers` with the value `47`
5. `emptyValue` with the value `null`

Example: `let color = "blue";` creates a variable called `color`.
hints: Each variable needs the `let` keyword, a name, an equals sign, and a value. Strings need quotes, numbers and booleans do not.
The pattern is `let name = value;` — make sure each declaration ends with a semicolon.

exercises.title: Reassign a Variable
exercises.description: Reassign variables declared with let to new values.
exercises.instructions:
Variables declared with `let` can be reassigned. To reassign, use just the variable name (no keyword) followed by `=` and the new value.

The starter code declares six variables. Reassign each one:
1. `status` from `"pending"` to `"complete"`
2. `count` from `10` to `count + 5` (should be 15)
3. `price` from `9.99` to `19.99`
4. `isActive` from `true` to `false`
5. `items` from `["a","b"]` to `["x","y","z"]`
6. `user` from `{name:"Alex"}` to `{name:"Sam",role:"admin"}`
hints: To reassign, write just the name followed by `=` and the new value — do not use `let` again.
For count, write `count = count + 5;` which takes the current value and adds 5.

exercises.title: Build a Map By Hand
exercises.description: Use a for loop to transform every element in an array into a new array.
exercises.instructions:
Before learning shortcut methods, practice the pattern they are built on.

Write a function called `doubleAll` that takes an array of numbers `nums` and returns a new array where every number is doubled.

Use a `for` loop — do NOT use `.map()` or `.forEach()`.

Example: `doubleAll([1, 2, 3])` returns `[2, 4, 6]`
Example: `doubleAll([5])` returns `[10]`
hints: Create an empty array first, then use a for loop to visit each element. Inside the loop, push the transformed value into the result array.
Declare `const result = [];` then loop with `for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++)` and inside use `result.push(nums[i] * 2);`.

exercises.title: Build a Filter By Hand
exercises.description: Use a for loop to select only matching elements from an array.
exercises.instructions:
Filtering means keeping only the elements that pass a test.

Write a function called `getEvens` that takes an array of numbers `nums` and returns a new array containing only the even numbers.

Use a `for` loop with an `if` statement — do NOT use `.filter()`.

Example: `getEvens([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])` returns `[2, 4]`
Example: `getEvens([7, 9])` returns `[]`
hints: Use the modulo operator (`%`) to check if a number is even. If `num % 2 === 0`, the number is even.
Inside your for loop, add `if (nums[i] % 2 === 0) { result.push(nums[i]); }` to keep only even numbers.

exercises.title: Convert to Arrow Function
exercises.description: Rewrite an ES5 function declaration as an arrow function.
exercises.instructions:
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write functions. Here is the conversion pattern:

**ES5:** `function name(param) { return value; }`
**Arrow:** `const name = (param) => { return value; };`

The function below is written in ES5 style:
```js
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

Rewrite it as an arrow function stored in a `const` called `double`.

Example: `double(5)` should return `10`
hints: Arrow functions replace the `function` keyword with `=>`. The function is stored in a variable using `const`.
Write `const double = (n) => { return n * 2; };` — the parameters go before the arrow, the body goes after.

exercises.title: Convert Loop to forEach
exercises.description: Rewrite a for loop as a forEach call.
hints: The `.forEach()` method takes a function as its argument. That function receives one element at a time, similar to how `words[i]` gives you one element.
Write `words.forEach(function(word) { result.push(word.toUpperCase()); });` — each `word` is like `words[i]` from the loop.

exercises.title: Array of Objects
exercises.description: Create an array that contains multiple objects.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays can hold any type of value — including objects. An array of objects is one of the most common data structures in programming.

Write a function called `getBooks` that returns an array containing 3 book objects. Each book should have:
- `title` (string)
- `author` (string)
- `year` (number)

The books should be:
1. `"1984"` by `"George Orwell"`, `1949`
2. `"Dune"` by `"Frank Herbert"`, `1965`
3. `"Neuromancer"` by `"William Gibson"`, `1984`

Example: `getBooks()[0].title` returns `"1984"`
hints: An array of objects looks like `[ { key: value }, { key: value }, { key: value } ]`. Each object is separated by a comma inside the square brackets.
Return `[{ title: "1984", author: "George Orwell", year: 1949 }, { title: "Dune", ... }, { ... }]`.

exercises.title: Nested Object
exercises.description: Create an object that contains another object as a property.
exercises.instructions:
An object property can hold any value — including another object. This is called nesting.

Write a function called `createStudent` that returns an object with:
- `name`: `"Maria"`
- `grade`: `10`
- `address`: an object with:
  - `city`: `"Tacoma"`
  - `state`: `"WA"`
  - `zip`: `"98402"`

Example: `createStudent().address.city` returns `"Tacoma"`
hints: A nested object is just an object inside another object. The inner object uses the same `{ key: value }` syntax as a regular object.
Set `address` to `{ city: "Tacoma", state: "WA", zip: "98402" }` inside the main object.

exercises.title: Declare a String
exercises.description: Declare five string variables using different quote styles.
exercises.instructions:
Strings hold text data in JavaScript. You can create strings using double quotes `"`, single quotes `'`, or backticks `` ` ``.

Declare five string variables using `const`:
1. `greeting` = `"Hello, world!"` (double quotes)
2. `language` = `'JavaScript'` (single quotes)
3. `message` = `` `Welcome back` `` (backticks)
4. `empty` = `""` (empty string)
5. `fullName` = `"Jane Doe"`
hints: Strings are text wrapped in quotes. JavaScript accepts double quotes, single quotes, and backticks.
Use `const name = "value";` for each — match the quote style shown for each variable.

exercises.title: Declare a Number
exercises.description: Declare five number variables including integers, decimals, and negatives.
exercises.instructions:
Numbers in JavaScript include integers, decimals, and negatives. Numbers do not use quotes.

Declare five number variables using `const`:
1. `score` = `95`
2. `price` = `19.99`
3. `temperature` = `-5`
4. `zero` = `0`
5. `population` = `7900000000`
hints: Numbers are written without quotes. Decimals use a dot, negatives use a minus sign.
Write `const score = 95;` for integers, `const price = 19.99;` for decimals.

exercises.title: Declare a Boolean
exercises.description: Declare five boolean variables using is/has/can naming conventions.
exercises.instructions:
Booleans represent `true` or `false`. By convention, boolean names start with `is`, `has`, or `can`.

Declare five booleans using `const`:
1. `isOnline` = `true`
2. `hasPermission` = `false`
3. `canEdit` = `true`
4. `isLoggedIn` = `false`
5. `hasCompleted` = `true`
hints: Booleans are `true` or `false` without quotes. Adding quotes makes them strings.
Use `const isOnline = true;` — the keywords `true` and `false` are lowercase.

exercises.title: Declare an Array
exercises.description: Declare four arrays containing different types of data.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays are ordered lists in square brackets `[]`. Items are separated by commas.

Declare four arrays using `const`:
1. `scores` = `[95, 87, 73, 100]`
2. `colors` = `["red", "green", "blue"]`
3. `mixed` = `[42, "hello", true, null]`
4. `empty` = `[]`
hints: Arrays use square brackets with items separated by commas.
Write `const scores = [95, 87, 73, 100];` — strings inside arrays still need quotes.

exercises.title: Declare an Object
exercises.description: Declare four objects with different property types.
exercises.instructions:
Objects store key-value pairs in curly braces `{}`. Each property has a name and value separated by a colon.

Declare four objects using `const`:
1. `student` = `{ name: "Alex", age: 25 }`
2. `dimensions` = `{ width: 100, height: 50 }`
3. `config` = `{ theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, isEnabled: true }`
4. `empty` = `{}`
hints: Objects use curly braces with `key: value` pairs separated by commas.
Write `const student = { name: "Alex", age: 25 };` — keys do not need quotes.

exercises.title: Naming Conventions
exercises.description: Declare ten variables following JavaScript naming conventions.
exercises.instructions:
JavaScript naming conventions:
- `camelCase` for regular variables
- `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for true constants
- `is`/`has`/`can` prefix for booleans

Declare these ten variables:
1. `firstName` = `"Maria"` (const)
2. `itemCount` = `0` (let)
3. `isVisible` = `true` (const)
4. `MAX_RETRIES` = `3` (const)
5. `shoppingCart` = `[]` (let)
6. `userProfile` = `{ name: "Alex", role: "student" }` (const)
7. `currentScore` = `85` (let)
8. `API_BASE_URL` = `"https://api.example.com"` (const)
9. `hasSeenWelcome` = `false` (let)
10. `defaultColor` = `"blue"` (const)
hints: camelCase means lowercase first word, uppercase each following word. True constants use ALL_CAPS.
Use `let` for changing values, `const` for fixed values. Booleans start with is/has/can.

exercises.title: Reassign an Array Element
exercises.description: Change individual elements inside an array using bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays are zero-indexed. Change elements with bracket notation: `array[index] = newValue;`

The starter code provides a colors array. Change:
1. `colors[0]` to `"crimson"`
2. `colors[2]` to `"navy"`
3. `colors[4]` to `"violet"`
4. `colors[1]` to `"lime"`
5. `colors[3]` to `"gold"`
hints: Array positions start at 0. The first item is `[0]`, second is `[1]`.
Write `colors[0] = "crimson";` to change the first element.

exercises.title: Reassign an Object Property
exercises.description: Change and add properties on an existing object using dot notation.
exercises.instructions:
Change properties with dot notation: `object.property = newValue;`. Add new properties the same way.

Make these changes to the car object:
1. `car.color` to `"blue"`
2. `car.year` to `2024`
3. `car.model` to `"Corolla"`
4. Add `car.mileage` = `15000`
5. Add `car.isElectric` = `false`
hints: Dot notation: `object.property = value;` to change existing or add new properties.
Write `car.color = "blue";` to change and `car.mileage = 15000;` to add.

exercises.title: Access an Array Element
exercises.description: Extract values from an array using bracket notation and zero-based indexing.
exercises.instructions:
Access elements with bracket notation: `array[index]`. First element is `[0]`.

The starter code provides a planets array. Extract:
1. `first` = `planets[0]`
2. `third` = `planets[2]`
3. `last` = `planets[4]`
4. `secondIndex` = `1`
5. `second` = `planets[secondIndex]`
6. `pair` = `planets[0] + " and " + planets[1]`
7. `totalPlanets` = `5`
hints: Use bracket notation with a number: `planets[0]` gets the first item.
A variable can be used as an index: `planets[secondIndex]` uses the value stored in secondIndex.

exercises.title: Access an Object Property
exercises.description: Extract values from an object using dot notation.
exercises.instructions:
Access properties with dot notation: `object.property`.

Extract from the book object:
1. `bookTitle` = `book.title`
2. `bookAuthor` = `book.author`
3. `publishYear` = `book.year`
4. `pageCount` = `book.pages`
5. `classic` = `book.isClassic`
6. `summary` = `book.title + " by " + book.author`
7. `age` = `2026 - book.year`
hints: Dot notation reads a property: `book.title` returns the value at the `title` key.
Use `+` to join strings: `book.title + " by " + book.author`.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: AND
exercises.description: Evaluate four AND expressions using the && operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `&&` (AND) operator returns `true` only when BOTH sides are `true`.

Using the source variables, evaluate:
1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn && hasPermission` (true && true)
2. `result2` = `isLoggedIn && isAdmin` (true && false)
3. `result3` = `isAdmin && hasPermission` (false && true)
4. `result4` = `isAdmin && isVerified` (false && false)
hints: The `&&` operator needs BOTH values to be `true` to produce `true`. If either side is `false`, the result is `false`.
Write `const result1 = isLoggedIn && hasPermission;` using the variable names from the starter code.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: OR
exercises.description: Evaluate four OR expressions using the || operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `||` (OR) operator returns `true` when at LEAST ONE side is `true`.

Using the source variables, evaluate:
1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn || hasPermission` (true || true)
2. `result2` = `isLoggedIn || isAdmin` (true || false)
3. `result3` = `isAdmin || hasPermission` (false || true)
4. `result4` = `isAdmin || isVerified` (false || false)
hints: The `||` operator only needs ONE side to be `true`. It only returns `false` when both are `false`.
Write `const result1 = isLoggedIn || hasPermission;` using the `||` operator between the two variables.

exercises.title: Logical Operator: NOT
exercises.description: Flip five boolean values using the ! operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `!` (NOT) operator flips a boolean: `true` becomes `false`, `false` becomes `true`.

Flip each value:
1. `result1` = `!isOnline` (flip true)
2. `result2` = `!isBlocked` (flip false)
3. `result3` = `!hasAccess` (flip true)
4. `result4` = `!isMuted` (flip false)
5. `result5` = `!isExpired` (flip true)
hints: The `!` goes directly before the value or variable name, with no space needed.
Write `const result1 = !isOnline;` to flip the boolean value.

exercises.title: Logical Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions that combine &&, ||, and ! operators.
exercises.instructions:
Combine logical operators in a single expression. `&&` is evaluated before `||` (like * before + in math).

1. `result1` = `isLoggedIn && hasPermission && isVerified`
2. `result2` = `isAdmin || hasPermission`
3. `result3` = `!isBanned && isLoggedIn`
4. `result4` = `isAdmin && !isBanned || hasPermission`
5. `result5` = `!(isLoggedIn && isAdmin)`
hints: When combining operators, `&&` runs before `||`. Use `!` to flip a single value before combining.
Use the exact variable names from the starter code and combine them with `&&`, `||`, and `!`.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Addition
exercises.description: Evaluate five addition expressions using the + operator.
hints: The `+` operator works with variables and literal numbers. You can add multiple values in one expression.
Write `const sum1 = a + b;` using the variable names provided.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Subtraction
exercises.description: Evaluate five subtraction expressions using the - operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `-` operator subtracts numbers. Results can be negative.

1. `diff1` = `a - b` (20 - 8 = 12)
2. `diff2` = `b - a` (8 - 20 = -12)
3. `diff3` = `c - a` (25 - 20 = 5)
4. `diff4` = `a - 3` (20 - 3 = 17)
5. `diff5` = `c - b - a` (25 - 8 - 20 = -3)
hints: Subtraction can produce negative results when the second number is larger.
Write `const diff1 = a - b;` — subtraction evaluates left to right.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Multiplication
exercises.description: Evaluate five multiplication expressions using the * operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `*` operator multiplies numbers.

1. `total` = `price * quantity` (25 * 4 = 100)
2. `doubled` = `price * 2` (25 * 2 = 50)
3. `tax` = `price * taxRate` (25 * 0.08 = 2)
4. `bulk` = `price * quantity * 2` (200)
5. `discounted` = `price * 0.9` (22.5)
hints: Multiplication uses `*` and works with decimals too. Multiple `*` operations chain together.
Write `const total = price * quantity;` using the variable names provided.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Division
exercises.description: Evaluate five division expressions using the / operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `/` operator divides numbers. Results can be decimals.

1. `perItem` = `total / items` (100 / 4 = 25)
2. `perPerson` = `total / people` (100 / 3 = 33.33...)
3. `half` = `total / 2` (50)
4. `quarter` = `total / 4` (25)
5. `tenth` = `total / 10` (10)
hints: Division uses `/` and can produce decimal results when the numbers do not divide evenly.
Write `const perItem = total / items;` — division evaluates left to right.

exercises.title: Math Operator: Modulo
exercises.description: Evaluate five modulo expressions using the % operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `%` (modulo) operator returns the remainder after division. Useful for checking even/odd.

1. `rem1` = `a % 5` (17 % 5 = 2)
2. `rem2` = `b % 3` (10 % 3 = 1)
3. `rem3` = `c % 2` (8 % 2 = 0, even)
4. `rem4` = `a % 2` (17 % 2 = 1, odd)
5. `rem5` = `a % b` (17 % 10 = 7)
hints: The `%` returns what is left over after dividing. Think: "17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2".
Write `const rem1 = a % 5;` — if the remainder is 0 the number divides evenly.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions following natural operator precedence.
exercises.instructions:
`*` and `/` are evaluated before `+` and `-`, just like in regular math.

1. `result1` = `a + b * c` (10 + 15 = 25)
2. `result2` = `a - b * c` (10 - 15 = -5)
3. `result3` = `a * b + c` (50 + 3 = 53)
4. `result4` = `a / b + c` (2 + 3 = 5)
5. `result5` = `a + b - c * 2` (10 + 5 - 6 = 9)
hints: Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just like in regular math.
Write the expression exactly as shown — do not add parentheses. Let natural precedence do the work.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Parentheses
exercises.description: Evaluate five expressions where parentheses override natural precedence.
exercises.instructions:
Parentheses `()` force operations inside them to happen first, overriding natural precedence.

1. `result1` = `(a + b) * c` (15 * 3 = 45)
2. `result2` = `a * (b + c)` (10 * 8 = 80)
3. `result3` = `(a - b) * (b - c)` (5 * 2 = 10)
4. `result4` = `a / (b - c)` (10 / 2 = 5)
5. `result5` = `(a + b + c) / 2` (18 / 2 = 9)
hints: Parentheses change the order: `(a + b) * c` adds first, then multiplies.
Write the expressions exactly as shown, with parentheses in the correct places.

exercises.title: Math Operators: Real-World Formulas
exercises.description: Calculate five real-world formulas using math operators and parentheses.
exercises.instructions:
Combine operators and parentheses to solve real-world formulas.

1. `celsius` = `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` (convert 98.6°F)
2. `average` = `(score1 + score2 + score3) / 3`
3. `salePrice` = `originalPrice - (originalPrice * discountPercent / 100)`
4. `totalWithTax` = `subtotal + (subtotal * taxPercent / 100)`
5. `simpleInterest` = `principal * rate * years / 100`
hints: Use parentheses to group the operations that need to happen first, just like in a math formula.
The Celsius formula is `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9` — subtract first, then multiply and divide.

exercises.title: Conditional: If
exercises.description: Write five if statements that change a variable when a condition is true.
exercises.instructions:
An `if` statement runs code only when its condition is `true`.

Syntax: `if (condition) { code }`

For each one, a default value is provided. Write an `if` statement that changes it:
1. `weather` starts as `"nice"` → if `temperature > 90`, set to `"hot"`
2. `grade` starts as `"pass"` → if `score < 50`, set to `"fail"`
3. `canDrive` starts as `"no"` → if `age >= 16`, set to `"yes"`
4. `status` starts as `"funded"` → if `balance === 0`, set to `"empty"`
5. `ticket` starts as `"none"` → if `speed > 65`, set to `"speeding"`
hints: An `if` statement checks a condition. If it is true, the code inside the curly braces runs.
Write `if (temperature > 90) { weather = "hot"; }` — the condition goes in parentheses.

exercises.title: Conditional: If Else
exercises.description: Write five if/else statements that choose between two values.
exercises.instructions:
An `if/else` statement chooses between two paths.

Syntax: `if (condition) { A } else { B }`

1. If `hour < 12` → `timeOfDay` = `"morning"`, else `"afternoon"`
2. If `temperature > 60` → `clothing` = `"shorts"`, else `"jacket"`
3. If `score >= 70` → `result` = `"pass"`, else `"fail"`
4. If `balance >= 100` → `canAfford` = `"yes"`, else `"no"`
5. If `age >= 21` → `beverage` = `"coffee or beer"`, else `"coffee"`
hints: `if/else` provides exactly two paths: one for when the condition is true, one for when it is false.
Write `if (hour < 12) { timeOfDay = "morning"; } else { timeOfDay = "afternoon"; }`

exercises.title: Conditional: If Else If Else
exercises.description: Write two multi-branch conditional chains using if/else if/else.
exercises.instructions:
`if/else if/else` chains check multiple conditions in order. The first match wins.

Chain 1 — Letter grade from `score` (82):
- >= 90 → `"A"`, >= 80 → `"B"`, >= 70 → `"C"`, >= 60 → `"D"`, else → `"F"`

Chain 2 — Weather advice from `temp` (45):
- >= 85 → `"Stay hydrated"`, >= 60 → `"Enjoy the weather"`, >= 32 → `"Wear a jacket"`, else → `"Stay inside"`
hints: Start with the highest threshold and work down. The first condition that is true sets the value.
Write `if (score >= 90) { grade = "A"; } else if (score >= 80) { grade = "B"; }` and continue the chain.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Loose Equality
exercises.description: Evaluate six loose equality expressions using the == operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `==` operator checks if values are equal, but converts types first (type coercion). This can cause surprises.

1. `result1` = `num == str` (5 == "5", true — number coerced)
2. `result2` = `zero == emptyStr` (0 == "", true — both falsy)
3. `result3` = `bool == one` (true == 1, true — bool becomes 1)
4. `result4` = `num == 10` (false)
5. `result5` = `zero == false` (0 == false, true)
6. `result6` = `null == undefined` (true — special case)
hints: `==` converts types before comparing. The number 5 and the string "5" are equal with `==` because of coercion.
Write `const result1 = num == str;` — use double equals for each comparison.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Strict Equality
exercises.description: Evaluate seven strict equality expressions using the === operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `===` operator checks both value AND type — no coercion. This is the recommended approach.

1. `result1` = `num === str` (5 === "5", false)
2. `result2` = `num === anotherFive` (5 === 5, true)
3. `result3` = `zero === emptyStr` (0 === "", false)
4. `result4` = `bool === one` (true === 1, false)
5. `result5` = `zero === false` (0 === false, false)
6. `result6` = `num === 5` (true)
7. `result7` = `str === "5"` (true)
hints: `===` requires both the value AND the type to match. The number 5 and string "5" are NOT equal with `===`.
Write `const result1 = num === str;` — use triple equals for each comparison.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Does Not Equal
exercises.description: Evaluate six strict inequality expressions using the !== operator.
exercises.instructions:
The `!==` operator returns `true` when values are NOT equal (or different types).

1. `result1` = `status !== "inactive"` (true)
2. `result2` = `count !== 0` (false)
3. `result3` = `role !== "admin"` (true)
4. `result4` = `score !== 100` (false)
5. `result5` = `theme !== "light"` (true)
6. `result6` = `limit !== 50` (false)
hints: `!==` is the opposite of `===` — it returns true when values are different.
Write `const result1 = status !== "inactive";` — if the values differ, the result is true.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Greater Than / Less Than
exercises.description: Evaluate seven expressions using the > and < operators.
exercises.instructions:
`>` returns true if left is greater. `<` returns true if left is less. Equal values return false for both.

1. `result1` = `age > 17` (true)
2. `result2` = `age < 21` (true)
3. `result3` = `price > 30` (false)
4. `result4` = `temperature < 80` (true)
5. `result5` = `speed > 55` (true)
6. `result6` = `age > 18` (false — equal, not greater)
7. `result7` = `age < 18` (false — equal, not less)
hints: `>` and `<` are strict — equal values return false. To include the boundary, use `>=` or `<=`.
Write `const result1 = age > 17;` — pay attention to the boundary cases with equal values.

exercises.title: Comparison Operator: Greater or Equal / Less or Equal
exercises.description: Evaluate seven expressions using the >= and <= operators.
exercises.instructions:
`>=` includes the boundary (greater than OR equal). `<=` includes the boundary (less than OR equal).

1. `result1` = `age >= 18` (true, at threshold)
2. `result2` = `age >= 21` (false)
3. `result3` = `balance <= 100` (true, at threshold)
4. `result4` = `balance <= 50` (false)
5. `result5` = `temperature >= 32` (true, at freezing)
6. `result6` = `score <= 100` (true)
7. `result7` = `score >= 70` (true, passing)
hints: `>=` and `<=` include the boundary value — they return true when values are exactly equal.
Write `const result1 = age >= 18;` — the `=` goes AFTER the `>` or `<`.

exercises.title: Comparison Operators: Combined
exercises.description: Evaluate six expressions that combine comparison and logical operators.
exercises.instructions:
Combine comparison (`>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `===`, `!==`) with logical (`&&`, `||`, `!`) operators.

1. `result1` = `age >= 18 && age <= 65` (working age)
2. `result2` = `score >= 90 || score <= 60` (high or low)
3. `result3` = `balance > 0 && balance < 100`
4. `result4` = `temperature >= 60 && temperature <= 80` (comfortable)
5. `result5` = `hour >= 9 && hour <= 17` (business hours)
6. `result6` = `!(age < 18) && score > 70`
hints: Range checks use `&&` to combine two comparisons: `value >= min && value <= max`.
Write `const result1 = age >= 18 && age <= 65;` — each comparison produces a boolean, then `&&` combines them.

exercises.title: Define a Function
exercises.description: Define a function that returns a greeting string.
exercises.instructions:
A function is a reusable block of code. Use the `function` keyword, give it a name, add parentheses `()`, and curly braces `{}`.

Define a function called `helloWorld` that returns the string `"Hello, World!"`.

Example: `function sayHi() { return "Hi!"; }`
hints: A function needs the `function` keyword, a name, parentheses, and curly braces. Use `return` to send a value back.
The structure is `function helloWorld() { return "Hello, World!"; }`

exercises.title: Define a Function with One Parameter
exercises.description: Define three functions that each accept one parameter.
exercises.instructions:
Parameters let a function receive input. The parameter goes inside the parentheses.

1. `greet(name)` — returns `"Hello, " + name + "!"`
2. `double(number)` — returns `number * 2`
3. `isPositive(number)` — returns `true` if `number > 0`
hints: Parameters are variables listed inside the parentheses. They receive the values passed when the function is called.
Fill in the return statement inside each function body using the parameter name.

exercises.title: Define a Function with Multiple Parameters
exercises.description: Define four functions that each accept multiple parameters.
exercises.instructions:
Functions can accept multiple parameters, separated by commas.

1. `add(a, b)` — returns `a + b`
2. `getFullName(first, last)` — returns `first + " " + last`
3. `isGreaterThan(a, b)` — returns `a > b`
4. `calculateArea(width, height)` — returns `width * height`
hints: Multiple parameters are separated by commas inside the parentheses.
Fill in the return statement: `return a + b;` for add, `return first + " " + last;` for getFullName.

exercises.title: Define a Function with a Default Parameter
exercises.description: Define three functions that use default parameter values.
exercises.instructions:
Default parameters provide a fallback value when no argument is passed.

Syntax: `function name(param = defaultValue) { }`

1. `greet(name = "World")` — returns `"Hello, " + name + "!"`
2. `double(number = 1)` — returns `number * 2`
3. `isOldEnough(age = 0)` — returns `age >= 18`
hints: Default values are set with `=` inside the parentheses: `function greet(name = "World")`.
Replace the comment with the parameter and its default: `name = "World"`, `number = 1`, `age = 0`.

exercises.title: Define a Function with Default Parameters
exercises.description: Define three functions that mix required and default parameters.
exercises.instructions:
When mixing required and default parameters, required parameters come first.

1. `greetPerson(name, greeting = "Hello")` — returns `greeting + ", " + name + "!"`
2. `add(a, b = 0)` — returns `a + b`
3. `multiply(a, b = 1)` — returns `a * b`
hints: Required parameters have no `=` sign. Default parameters use `=` to set a fallback value.
Add `= "Hello"` after greeting, `= 0` after b in add, `= 1` after b in multiply.

exercises.title: Write a For Loop
exercises.description: Write for loops that count and accumulate values.
exercises.instructions:
A for loop repeats code a set number of times.

Syntax: `for (let i = start; i < end; i++) { }`

1. Create `sum` = `0`, loop from 1 to 5 adding each number. Result: 15
2. Create `countdown` = `""`, loop from 5 to 1 adding each number + space. Result: `"5 4 3 2 1 "`
3. Create `evenSum` = `0`, loop from 0 to 10 by 2 adding each. Result: 30
hints: A for loop has three parts in the parentheses: starting value, condition to keep going, and how to update.
For counting up: `for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++)`. For counting down: `for (let i = 5; i >= 1; i--)`.

exercises.title: For Loop: Count Up
exercises.description: Write a function that counts from 1 to 10 using a for loop.
exercises.instructions:
Write the loop body inside the provided function skeleton.

The function should build a string of numbers from 1 to 10 separated by spaces.
hints: Start with an empty string, then use the loop to add each number followed by a space.
Create `let result = "";` then `for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { result = result + i + " "; }` then return result.

exercises.title: For Loop: Count Down
exercises.description: Write a function that counts from 10 down to 1 using a for loop.
exercises.instructions:
Write the loop body inside the provided function skeleton.

The function should build a string counting down from 10 to 1.
hints: To count down, start high, check >= low, and use `i--` to subtract 1 each time.
Use `for (let i = 10; i >= 1; i--)` — the `i--` decreases i by 1 each iteration.

exercises.title: For Loop: Custom Steps
exercises.description: Write a function that counts by fives from 5 to 50 using a for loop.
exercises.instructions: Use a custom step size to skip numbers. Instead of `i++`, use `i += 5` to jump by 5.
hints: Instead of `i++` which adds 1, use `i += 5` to add 5 each time through the loop.
Use `for (let i = 5; i <= 50; i += 5)` to start at 5 and jump by 5 each iteration.

exercises.title: For Loop: Dynamic Range
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a number range using loop parameters.
exercises.instructions: Functions can control loops using their parameters. Add three parameters to the function: `start`, `stop`, and `step`.
hints: The function needs three parameters that control the loop: where to start, where to stop, and how much to add each time.
Add `start, stop, step` in the parentheses, then use them in the for loop: `for (let i = start; i <= stop; i += step)`.

exercises.title: Assignment Operators
exercises.description: Use compound assignment operators to update variable values.
exercises.instructions:
Assignment operators combine an operation with assignment:
- `+=` adds and assigns
- `-=` subtracts and assigns
- `*=` multiplies and assigns
- `/=` divides and assigns
- `%=` gets remainder and assigns

Apply these operators to `score` (starts at 100) and `count` (starts at 0).
hints: Each operator combines the operation with `=`: `score += 25` is the same as `score = score + 25`.
Write `score += 25;` then `score -= 10;` then `score *= 2;` and so on for each step.

exercises.title: Loop Styles: for...in
exercises.description: Complete a for...in loop that iterates over object keys.
exercises.instructions:
A `for...in` loop iterates over the keys (property names) of an object.

Syntax: `for (let key in object) { }`

Replace the blanks `__keyVariable__` and `__objectName__` to complete the loop.
hints: Replace the blanks with a variable name for the key and the name of the object to loop over.
Use `key` for the key variable and `scores` for the object. Inside the loop, `scores[key]` gets each value.

exercises.title: Loop Styles: for...of
exercises.description: Complete a for...of loop that iterates over array values.
exercises.instructions:
A `for...of` loop iterates over the values of an array.

Syntax: `for (let value of array) { }`

Replace the blanks `__valueVariable__` and `__arrayName__` to complete the loop.
hints: Replace the blanks with a variable name for each value and the name of the array to loop over.
Use `fruit` for the value variable and `fruits` for the array. Each iteration, `fruit` holds the next array value.

exercises.title: Loop Styles: while
exercises.description: Complete a while loop that repeats until a condition is false.
exercises.instructions:
A `while` loop repeats as long as a condition is `true`.

Syntax: `while (condition) { }` — you must update the condition inside the loop!

Replace `__condition__` and `__updateStep__` to count down from 5 to 1.
hints: The condition should check if countdown is still positive. The update step should decrease countdown by 1.
Use `countdown > 0` for the condition and `countdown = countdown - 1` for the update step.

exercises.title: Loop Styles: do...while
exercises.description: Complete a do...while loop that runs at least once before checking its condition.
exercises.instructions:
A `do...while` loop runs the code block first, then checks the condition. This guarantees the body runs at least once.

Syntax: `do { } while (condition);`

Replace `__updateStep__` and `__condition__` to count from 1 to 5.
hints: The update step increases number by 1. The condition keeps the loop going while number is 5 or less.
Use `number = number + 1` for the update and `number <= 5` for the condition.

exercises.title: String Concatenation
exercises.description: Build strings by joining values together with the + operator.
exercises.instructions:
String concatenation joins strings using the `+` operator. You can combine strings, variables, and numbers.

Build these five strings using ONLY the `+` operator (no backticks):
1. `fullName` = `"Jane Doe"`
2. `bio` = `"Jane is 28 years old."`
3. `location` = `"Jane Doe lives in Seattle."`
4. `profile` = `"Name: Jane Doe, Age: 28"`
5. `greeting` = `"Hello, my name is Jane and I am from Seattle!"`
hints: Use `+` to join pieces together. Include literal strings for spaces and punctuation between variables.
Write `firstName + " " + lastName` to join with a space. Numbers convert to strings automatically when concatenated.

exercises.title: String Interpolation
exercises.description: Build strings using template literal interpolation with backticks and ${} syntax.
exercises.instructions:
Template literals use backticks `` ` `` and `${}` to embed variables directly in a string. This is called string interpolation.

Build the same five strings using ONLY backticks and `${}` (no `+` concatenation):
1. `fullName` — `"Jane Doe"`
2. `bio` — `"Jane is 28 years old."`
3. `location` — `"Jane Doe lives in Seattle."`
4. `profile` — `"Name: Jane Doe, Age: 28"`
5. `greeting` — `"Hello, my name is Jane and I am from Seattle!"`
hints: Template literals use backticks instead of quotes. Inside backticks, `${variableName}` embeds the variable value.
Write `` `${firstName} ${lastName}` `` — the `${}` syntax replaces itself with the variable value.

exercises.title: Math Object: Rounding
exercises.description: Use Math.round, Math.floor, and Math.ceil to round numbers.
exercises.instructions:
The Math object provides built-in rounding methods:
- `Math.round()` — round to nearest integer
- `Math.floor()` — round DOWN
- `Math.ceil()` — round UP

1. `roundedPrice` = `Math.round(price)` → 10
2. `floorTemp` = `Math.floor(temperature)` → 72
3. `ceilTemp` = `Math.ceil(temperature)` → 73
4. `roundedRating` = `Math.round(rating)` → 5
5. `floorPrice` = `Math.floor(price)` → 9
hints: `Math.round()` rounds to nearest, `Math.floor()` always rounds down, `Math.ceil()` always rounds up.
Write `const roundedPrice = Math.round(price);` — pass the value inside the parentheses.

exercises.title: Math Object: Utilities
exercises.description: Use Math utility methods to perform common calculations.
exercises.instructions:
Math utility methods:
- `Math.abs()` — absolute value
- `Math.min()` — smallest of given numbers
- `Math.max()` — largest of given numbers
- `Math.pow(base, exp)` — raise to power
- `Math.sqrt()` — square root

1. `absolute` = `Math.abs(a)` → 15
2. `smallest` = `Math.min(a, b, c, d)` → -15
3. `largest` = `Math.max(a, b, c, d)` → 23
4. `cubed` = `Math.pow(b, 3)` → 343
5. `root` = `Math.sqrt(144)` → 12
