hints: Each method starts with `Math.` followed by the method name and parentheses containing the values.
Write `const absolute = Math.abs(a);` — pass variables or numbers as arguments to each method.

exercises.title: isEven
exercises.description: Write a function that checks if a number is even.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isEven` that takes a number and returns `true` if it is even, `false` otherwise.

A number is even if dividing by 2 leaves no remainder. Use the modulo operator `%`.

Example: `isEven(4)` returns `true`, `isEven(7)` returns `false`.
hints: The modulo operator `%` gives the remainder after division. Even numbers have no remainder when divided by 2.
Check if `number % 2 === 0` and return the result.

exercises.title: isOdd
exercises.description: Write a function that checks if a number is odd.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isOdd` that takes a number and returns `true` if it is odd, `false` otherwise.

A number is odd if dividing by 2 leaves a remainder of 1.

Example: `isOdd(3)` returns `true`, `isOdd(8)` returns `false`.
hints: Odd numbers have a remainder when divided by 2. Use `%` to check.
Check if `number % 2 !== 0` and return the result.

exercises.title: canVote
exercises.description: Write a function that checks if a person is old enough to vote.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `canVote` that takes an `age` and returns `true` if the age is 18 or older, `false` otherwise.

Example: `canVote(21)` returns `true`, `canVote(16)` returns `false`.
hints: Compare the age to 18 using a comparison operator.
Use `>=` to check if age is greater than or equal to 18.

exercises.title: isInRange
exercises.description: Write a function that checks if a number is within a range.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isInRange` that takes three parameters: `number`, `min`, and `max`. Return `true` if the number is between min and max (inclusive), `false` otherwise.

Example: `isInRange(5, 1, 10)` returns `true`, `isInRange(15, 1, 10)` returns `false`.
hints: You need two conditions: the number must be at least the min AND at most the max.
Use `number >= min && number <= max` to check both bounds.

exercises.title: largerOf
exercises.description: Write a function that returns the larger of two numbers.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `largerOf` that takes two numbers and returns the larger one.

Example: `largerOf(5, 9)` returns `9`, `largerOf(12, 3)` returns `12`.
hints: Compare the two numbers with `if` and return the appropriate one.
Use `if (a >= b) { return a; } else { return b; }` to pick the larger value.

exercises.title: smallerOf
exercises.description: Write a function that returns the smaller of two numbers.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `smallerOf` that takes two numbers and returns the smaller one.

Example: `smallerOf(5, 9)` returns `5`, `smallerOf(12, 3)` returns `3`.
hints: Compare the two numbers with `if` and return the appropriate one.
Use `if (a <= b) { return a; } else { return b; }` to pick the smaller value.

exercises.title: getSign
exercises.description: Write a function that returns the sign of a number as a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getSign` that takes a number and returns:
- `"positive"` if the number is greater than 0
- `"negative"` if the number is less than 0
- `"zero"` if the number is 0

Example: `getSign(5)` returns `"positive"`, `getSign(-3)` returns `"negative"`.
hints: You need three branches: one for positive, one for negative, one for zero.
Use `if (number > 0)` for positive, `else if (number < 0)` for negative, `else` for zero.

exercises.title: getGrade
exercises.description: Write a function that converts a numeric score to a letter grade.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getGrade` that takes a `score` (0-100) and returns a letter grade:
- 90 or above: `"A"`
- 80-89: `"B"`
- 70-79: `"C"`
- 60-69: `"D"`
- Below 60: `"F"`

Example: `getGrade(95)` returns `"A"`, `getGrade(73)` returns `"C"`.
hints: Start with the highest grade and work down. Each `else if` only runs if all previous conditions were false.
Use `if (score >= 90)` then `else if (score >= 80)` and so on down to `else` for F.

exercises.title: ticketPrice
exercises.description: Write a function that returns a ticket price based on age.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `ticketPrice` that takes an `age` and returns the ticket price:
- Under 3: `0` (free)
- 3-12: `8`
- 13-64: `15`
- 65 or older: `10`

Example: `ticketPrice(2)` returns `0`, `ticketPrice(30)` returns `15`.
hints: Think about the age brackets from youngest to oldest. Each bracket has a different price.
Use `if (age < 3)` for free, `else if (age <= 12)` for child, `else if (age <= 64)` for adult, `else` for senior.

exercises.title: clamp
exercises.description: Write a function that clamps a number within a range.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `clamp` that takes three parameters: `number`, `min`, and `max`. Return:
- `min` if the number is below min
- `max` if the number is above max
- The number itself if it is within range

Example: `clamp(5, 1, 10)` returns `5`, `clamp(-3, 0, 100)` returns `0`.
hints: Check if the number is below the minimum or above the maximum, and return the boundary if so.
Use `if (number < min) return min; else if (number > max) return max; else return number;`

exercises.title: fizzBuzz
exercises.description: Write a function that returns Fizz, Buzz, or FizzBuzz for a number.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `fizzBuzz` that takes a number and returns:
- `"FizzBuzz"` if divisible by both 3 and 5
- `"Fizz"` if divisible by 3 only
- `"Buzz"` if divisible by 5 only
- The number as a string otherwise

Example: `fizzBuzz(15)` returns `"FizzBuzz"`, `fizzBuzz(9)` returns `"Fizz"`.
hints: The order of checks matters. Check the combined condition (divisible by both 3 AND 5) first.
Use `number % 3 === 0 && number % 5 === 0` for FizzBuzz, then check each separately. Use `String(number)` for the default.

exercises.title: toCelsius
exercises.description: Write a function that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `toCelsius` that takes a temperature in Fahrenheit and returns the equivalent in Celsius.

Formula: `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9`

Example: `toCelsius(32)` returns `0`, `toCelsius(212)` returns `100`.
hints: Apply the formula step by step: subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5, then divide by 9.
Use parentheses to ensure subtraction happens first: `(fahrenheit - 32) * 5 / 9`.

exercises.title: toFahrenheit
exercises.description: Write a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `toFahrenheit` that takes a temperature in Celsius and returns the equivalent in Fahrenheit.

Formula: `celsius * 9 / 5 + 32`

Example: `toFahrenheit(0)` returns `32`, `toFahrenheit(100)` returns `212`.
hints: Apply the formula: multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32.
Write `return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32;` — JavaScript evaluates multiplication and division before addition.

exercises.title: areaOfCircle
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates the area of a circle.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `areaOfCircle` that takes a `radius` and returns the area.

Formula: `Math.PI * radius * radius`

Example: `areaOfCircle(1)` returns approximately `3.14159`.
hints: The area of a circle is pi times the radius squared. JavaScript provides `Math.PI` for pi.
Write `return Math.PI * radius * radius;` to calculate the area.

exercises.title: hypotenuse
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `hypotenuse` that takes two sides `a` and `b` and returns the length of the hypotenuse.

Formula: `Math.sqrt(a * a + b * b)`

Example: `hypotenuse(3, 4)` returns `5`.
hints: The Pythagorean theorem says c = square root of (a squared + b squared). Use `Math.sqrt()`.
Write `return Math.sqrt(a * a + b * b);` to calculate the hypotenuse.

exercises.title: calculateTip
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates a tip amount.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `calculateTip` that takes a `bill` amount and a `tipPercent` (as a whole number like 15, 20) and returns the tip amount.

Formula: `bill * tipPercent / 100`

Example: `calculateTip(50, 20)` returns `10`.
hints: To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide by 100. Then multiply by the bill.
Write `return bill * tipPercent / 100;` to calculate the tip.

exercises.title: coinTotal
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates the dollar value of coins.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `coinTotal` that takes four parameters: `quarters`, `dimes`, `nickels`, and `pennies`. Return the total value in dollars.

Values: quarter = $0.25, dime = $0.10, nickel = $0.05, penny = $0.01.

Example: `coinTotal(4, 0, 0, 0)` returns `1` (four quarters = $1.00).
hints: Multiply each coin count by its dollar value and add them all together.
Write `return quarters * 0.25 + dimes * 0.10 + nickels * 0.05 + pennies * 0.01;`

exercises.title: calculateShipping
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates shipping cost based on order total.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `calculateShipping` that takes an `orderTotal` and returns the shipping cost:
- Orders $50 or more: `0` (free shipping)
- Orders $25-$49.99: `5`
- Orders under $25: `10`

Example: `calculateShipping(60)` returns `0`, `calculateShipping(30)` returns `5`.
hints: Check the order total against the thresholds, starting with the highest.
Use `if (orderTotal >= 50)` for free, `else if (orderTotal >= 25)` for $5, `else` for $10.

exercises.title: factorial
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates the factorial of a number.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `factorial` that takes a number `n` and returns its factorial (n!).

The factorial is the product of all positive integers up to n. Use a `for` loop.

`factorial(5)` = 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = `120`
`factorial(0)` = `1` (by definition).
hints: Start with a result variable set to 1, then use a loop to multiply it by each number from 1 to n.
Create `let result = 1;` then loop `for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++)` and inside do `result = result * i;`.

exercises.title: power
exercises.description: Write a function that raises a base to an exponent using a loop.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `power` that takes a `base` and `exponent` and returns `base` raised to the `exponent`.

Use a `for` loop — do not use `Math.pow()` or `**`.

`power(2, 3)` = 2 * 2 * 2 = `8`
`power(5, 0)` = `1` (anything to the power of 0 is 1).
hints: Start with a result of 1, then multiply by the base once for each unit of the exponent.
Create `let result = 1;` then loop `for (let i = 0; i < exponent; i++)` and inside do `result = result * base;`.

exercises.title: repeatString
exercises.description: Write a function that repeats a string a given number of times.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `repeatString` that takes a `str` and a `times` count. Use a `for` loop to build a new string by concatenating `str` that many times.

Example: `repeatString("ha", 3)` returns `"hahaha"`.
hints: Start with an empty string and add to it inside a loop that runs the right number of times.
Create `let result = "";` then loop `for (let i = 0; i < times; i++)` and inside do `result = result + str;`.

exercises.title: countEvens
exercises.description: Write a function that counts even numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countEvens` that takes a number `n` and returns how many even numbers there are from 1 to `n` (inclusive).

Use a `for` loop and an `if` statement.

Example: `countEvens(10)` returns `5` (2, 4, 6, 8, 10).
hints: Use a counter variable starting at 0, loop from 1 to n, and check each number with the modulo operator.
Inside the loop, use `if (i % 2 === 0) { count = count + 1; }` to count even numbers.

exercises.title: countOdds
exercises.description: Write a function that counts odd numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countOdds` that takes a number `n` and returns how many odd numbers there are from 1 to `n` (inclusive).

Example: `countOdds(10)` returns `5` (1, 3, 5, 7, 9).
hints: Similar to counting evens, but check for odd numbers instead.
Inside the loop, use `if (i % 2 !== 0) { count = count + 1; }` to count odd numbers.

exercises.title: sumEvens
exercises.description: Write a function that sums all even numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `sumEvens` that takes a number `n` and returns the sum of all even numbers from 1 to `n` (inclusive).

Example: `sumEvens(10)` returns `30` (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10).
hints: Use an accumulator variable starting at 0, loop from 1 to n, and add even numbers to it.
Inside the loop, use `if (i % 2 === 0) { sum = sum + i; }` to accumulate even numbers.

exercises.title: sumOdds
exercises.description: Write a function that sums all odd numbers from 1 to n.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `sumOdds` that takes a number `n` and returns the sum of all odd numbers from 1 to `n` (inclusive).

Example: `sumOdds(10)` returns `25` (1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9).
hints: Same pattern as sumEvens, but check for odd numbers instead.
Inside the loop, use `if (i % 2 !== 0) { sum = sum + i; }` to accumulate odd numbers.

exercises.title: isLeapYear
exercises.description: Write a function that checks if a year is a leap year.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isLeapYear` that takes a `year` and returns `true` if it is a leap year, `false` otherwise.

Leap year rules:
- Divisible by 4 → leap year
- EXCEPT divisible by 100 → not a leap year
- EXCEPT divisible by 400 → leap year

Example: `isLeapYear(2024)` returns `true`, `isLeapYear(1900)` returns `false`.
hints: Check the most specific rule first (divisible by 400), then the exception (divisible by 100), then the base rule (divisible by 4).
Start with `if (year % 400 === 0) return true;` then `else if (year % 100 === 0) return false;` then `else if (year % 4 === 0) return true;` then `else return false;`.

exercises.title: bottleSong
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a countdown song lyric.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `bottleSong` that takes a starting `count` and returns a string with each line counting down.

Each line follows the pattern: `"N bottles on the wall"` (where N counts down to 1).
Lines are separated by a newline character `"\n"`.

Example: `bottleSong(3)` returns:
`"3 bottles on the wall\n2 bottles on the wall\n1 bottles on the wall"`
hints: Use a for loop that counts down. Build up the result string by adding each line and a newline separator between lines.
Loop `for (let i = count; i >= 1; i--)` and add `i + " bottles on the wall"`. Add `"\n"` between lines but not after the last one.

exercises.title: dashJoin
exercises.description: Write a function that joins numbers with dashes.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `dashJoin` that takes a number `n` and returns a string of numbers from 1 to n joined by dashes.

Example: `dashJoin(5)` returns `"1-2-3-4-5"`, `dashJoin(1)` returns `"1"`.
hints: Build a string in a loop, adding a dash separator between numbers but not after the last one.
Loop from 1 to n. Add the number to result, then add a dash only if `i < n`.

exercises.title: multiplicationRow
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a multiplication table row.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `multiplicationRow` that takes a `number` and returns a string showing that number multiplied by 1 through 5.

Format each entry as `"N x M = P"` separated by `", "`.

Example: `multiplicationRow(3)` returns `"3 x 1 = 3, 3 x 2 = 6, 3 x 3 = 9, 3 x 4 = 12, 3 x 5 = 15"`.
hints: Use a loop from 1 to 5. Build each entry by concatenating the number, " x ", the loop counter, " = ", and the product.
Inside the loop: `result = result + number + " x " + i + " = " + (number * i);` and add `", "` between entries.

exercises.title: buildOdds
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a string of odd numbers in a range.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `buildOdds` that takes a number `n` and returns a string of all odd numbers from 1 to `n`, separated by spaces.

Example: `buildOdds(10)` returns `"1 3 5 7 9"`, `buildOdds(7)` returns `"1 3 5 7"`.
hints: Loop from 1 to n, check if each number is odd, and if so add it to the result with a space separator.
Check `if (i % 2 !== 0)` to find odd numbers. Add a space before each number except the first.

exercises.title: maxOfThree
exercises.description: Write a function that returns the largest of three numbers.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `maxOfThree` that takes three numbers `a`, `b`, and `c` and returns the largest.

Example: `maxOfThree(5, 9, 3)` returns `9`, `maxOfThree(1, 1, 1)` returns `1`.
hints: Compare each value against the other two to find which is the largest.
Check `if (a >= b && a >= c)` return a, `else if (b >= a && b >= c)` return b, `else` return c.

exercises.title: discountPrice
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates a discounted price.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `discountPrice` that takes a `price` and a `discount` percentage (whole number like 20, 50). Return the price after the discount is applied.

If the discount is greater than 100, return `0` (price cannot be negative).

Example: `discountPrice(100, 20)` returns `80`, `discountPrice(50, 150)` returns `0`.
hints: First handle the edge case where discount exceeds 100. Then calculate the discount amount and subtract it from the price.
Check `if (discount > 100) return 0;` then `return price - (price * discount / 100);`.

exercises.title: celsiusLabel
exercises.description: Write a function that returns a temperature label based on Celsius.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `celsiusLabel` that takes a Celsius temperature and returns a descriptive label:
- 30 or above: `"hot"`
- 20-29: `"warm"`
- 10-19: `"cool"`
- Below 10: `"cold"`

Example: `celsiusLabel(35)` returns `"hot"`, `celsiusLabel(15)` returns `"cool"`.
hints: Check from the highest temperature bracket down, using if/else if/else.
Use `if (celsius >= 30)` for hot, `else if (celsius >= 20)` for warm, `else if (celsius >= 10)` for cool, `else` for cold.

exercises.title: calculateTax
exercises.description: Write a function that calculates tax with a default rate.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `calculateTax` that takes a `price` and an optional `taxRate` (default `0.08` for 8%). Return the total price including tax.

Formula: `price + (price * taxRate)`

Example: `calculateTax(100)` returns `108`, `calculateTax(100, 0.10)` returns `110`.
hints: The default parameter value is used when no argument is provided. Calculate the total by adding the tax amount to the price.
Write `return price + (price * taxRate);` — when called without a second argument, taxRate defaults to 0.08.

exercises.title: countdown
exercises.description: Write a function that counts down from a starting number.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countdown` that takes an optional `start` (default `5`) and returns a string counting down to 1, separated by spaces, ending with `"Go!"`.

Example: `countdown()` returns `"5 4 3 2 1 Go!"`, `countdown(3)` returns `"3 2 1 Go!"`.
hints: Use a for loop counting down from start to 1, building a string with spaces. Then append "Go!" at the end.
Loop `for (let i = start; i >= 1; i--)` adding each number and a space, then add "Go!" after the loop.

exercises.title: convertDistance
exercises.description: Write a function that converts miles to kilometers with an optional rate.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `convertDistance` that takes `miles` and an optional `rate` (default `1.60934`) and returns the distance in kilometers.

Formula: `miles * rate`

Example: `convertDistance(1)` returns approximately `1.60934`, `convertDistance(10)` returns approximately `16.0934`.
hints: Multiply miles by the rate. The default rate converts miles to kilometers.
Write `return miles * rate;` — when called without a second argument, rate defaults to 1.60934.

exercises.title: buildSequence
exercises.description: Write a function that builds a number sequence with a default step.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `buildSequence` that takes a `count` and optional `step` (default `1`). Return a string of numbers starting from `step`, increasing by `step`, for `count` terms, separated by commas.

Example: `buildSequence(5)` returns `"1,2,3,4,5"`, `buildSequence(4, 3)` returns `"3,6,9,12"`.
hints: Each term in the sequence is the loop counter multiplied by the step. Build the string with commas between terms.
Loop from 1 to count. Each value is `i * step`. Add commas between values using `if (i < count)`.

exercises.title: generateMultiples
exercises.description: Write a function that generates multiples of a number.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `generateMultiples` that takes a `base` and optional `count` (default `5`). Return a string of the first `count` multiples of `base`, separated by spaces.

Example: `generateMultiples(7)` returns `"7 14 21 28 35"`, `generateMultiples(3, 3)` returns `"3 6 9"`.
hints: Each multiple is the base multiplied by the position (1, 2, 3, ...). Build the string with spaces between values.
Loop from 1 to count. Each value is `base * i`. Add spaces between values using `if (i < count)`.

exercises.title: Switch Statement
exercises.description: Return the name of a day using a switch statement.
exercises.instructions:
A `switch` statement compares a value against multiple `case` labels and runs the matching block. Each case needs a `break` (or `return`) to stop execution from continuing to the next case. A `default` case handles values that don't match any case.

Write a function called `getDayName` that takes a `dayNumber` (1-7) and returns the day name:
- 1 = `"Monday"`, 2 = `"Tuesday"`, 3 = `"Wednesday"`, 4 = `"Thursday"`, 5 = `"Friday"`, 6 = `"Saturday"`, 7 = `"Sunday"`
- Return `"Invalid day"` for any other number.

Example: `getDayName(1)` returns `"Monday"`, `getDayName(6)` returns `"Saturday"`.
hints: A switch compares one value against many possible matches. Think of it as a cleaner way to write many if/else-if checks.
Each `case` label is followed by a colon, then the code to run. Use `return` to exit the function from each case.

exercises.title: Switch: Fall-Through
exercises.description: Use switch fall-through to group days into weekday or weekend.
exercises.instructions:
When a `case` does not have a `break` or `return`, execution "falls through" to the next case. This lets you group multiple cases that share the same result.

Write a function called `getWeekdayType` that takes a `dayNumber` (1-7) and returns:
- `"weekday"` for days 1-5
- `"weekend"` for days 6-7
- `"Invalid day"` for anything else

Example: `getWeekdayType(3)` returns `"weekday"`, `getWeekdayType(6)` returns `"weekend"`.
hints: Fall-through means stacking cases without a break or return between them. All stacked cases run the same code.
List cases 1 through 5 one after another with no return until after case 5, then do the same for 6 and 7.

exercises.title: Switch: Fall-Through
exercises.description: Use switch fall-through to map months to fiscal quarters.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getQuarter` that takes a `month` number (1-12) and returns the fiscal quarter:
- Months 1-3: `"Q1"`
- Months 4-6: `"Q2"`
- Months 7-9: `"Q3"`
- Months 10-12: `"Q4"`
- Anything else: `"Invalid month"`

Use fall-through to group three months per quarter.

Example: `getQuarter(2)` returns `"Q1"`, `getQuarter(11)` returns `"Q4"`.
hints: Group three months per quarter using fall-through. Each group of three shares one return statement.
Stack `case 1: case 2: case 3: return "Q1";` on one line, then repeat the pattern for each quarter.

exercises.title: Switch: String Matching
exercises.description: Use a switch statement to match string values to coin amounts.
exercises.instructions:
Switch statements can match strings, not just numbers.

Write a function called `getCoinValue` that takes a `coin` name and returns its value in cents:
- `"penny"` → `1`
- `"nickel"` → `5`
- `"dime"` → `10`
- `"quarter"` → `25`
- Any other string → `0`

Example: `getCoinValue("dime")` returns `10`, `getCoinValue("dollar")` returns `0`.
hints: Switch works the same with strings as with numbers — each case label is a string value to match against.
Write `case "penny": return 1;` for each coin. The default case handles anything that does not match.

exercises.title: Switch: Default
exercises.description: Use a switch with a meaningful default case for HTTP status codes.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getHttpStatus` that takes a status `code` and returns its description:
- `200` → `"OK"`
- `301` → `"Moved Permanently"`
- `404` → `"Not Found"`
- `500` → `"Internal Server Error"`
- Any other code → `"Unknown Status"`

The `default` case handles all codes not explicitly listed.

Example: `getHttpStatus(404)` returns `"Not Found"`, `getHttpStatus(418)` returns `"Unknown Status"`.
hints: The default case catches everything that does not match a specific case. Think of it like the final `else` in an if/else chain.
List the known status codes as cases with their descriptions, then use `default` for everything else.

exercises.title: Ternary Operator
exercises.description: Return the absolute value of a number using a ternary expression.
exercises.instructions:
The ternary operator is a shorthand for a simple if/else. It uses `?` and `:` to choose between two values based on a condition.

Syntax: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`

Write a function called `absolute` that takes a `number` and returns its absolute value (distance from zero). If the number is negative, negate it. Otherwise, return it unchanged.

Example: `absolute(-5)` returns `5`, `absolute(3)` returns `3`.
hints: The ternary has three parts: a condition, a value when true, and a value when false, separated by `?` and `:`.
The condition is `number < 0`. If true, return the negated number. If false, return the number as-is.

exercises.title: Ternary: Inline
exercises.description: Use a ternary inside a string expression to format a price.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `feeOrFree` that takes a boolean `isMember` and a `price` number. Return:
- `"Free"` if `isMember` is `true`
- `"$"` followed by the price if `isMember` is `false`

Example: `feeOrFree(true, 9.99)` returns `"Free"`, `feeOrFree(false, 25)` returns `"$25"`.
hints: The ternary can be used anywhere a value is expected, including as the return value of a function.
Return `isMember ? "Free" : "$" + price` — the ternary picks which value to return.

exercises.title: Ternary: Chained
exercises.description: Use a chained ternary to classify an age into three groups.
exercises.instructions:
Ternary expressions can be chained to handle more than two outcomes. The "false" branch of the first ternary becomes another ternary.

Pattern: `condition1 ? value1 : condition2 ? value2 : value3`

Write a function called `classifyAge` that takes an `age` and returns:
- `"child"` if under 13
- `"teen"` if 13-17
- `"adult"` if 18 or older

Example: `classifyAge(8)` returns `"child"`, `classifyAge(15)` returns `"teen"`.
hints: Chain ternaries by placing another ternary in the "false" position of the first one.
The pattern reads left to right: `age < 13 ? "child" : age < 18 ? "teen" : "adult"`.

exercises.title: Ternary: Chained
exercises.description: Use a deeper chained ternary to classify a score into four labels.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `scoreLabel` that takes a `score` (0-100) and returns:
- `"excellent"` if 90 or above
- `"good"` if 70-89
- `"average"` if 50-69
- `"poor"` if below 50

Use a single chained ternary expression.

Example: `scoreLabel(95)` returns `"excellent"`, `scoreLabel(42)` returns `"poor"`.
hints: Extend the chaining pattern: each "false" branch can be another condition-value pair, ending with the final fallback value.
Read left to right: `score >= 90 ? "excellent" : score >= 70 ? "good" : score >= 50 ? "average" : "poor"`.

exercises.title: Nested If
exercises.description: Validate triangle sides and then classify the triangle type.
exercises.instructions:
A nested conditional places one `if` inside another. This is useful when you need to validate input before processing it.

Write a function called `classifyTriangle` that takes three side lengths `a`, `b`, and `c`.

First, check if the sides form a valid triangle:
- All sides must be positive
- The sum of any two sides must be greater than the third

If invalid, return `"invalid"`.

If valid, classify:
- All three sides equal → `"equilateral"`
- Exactly two sides equal → `"isosceles"`
- All sides different → `"scalene"`

Example: `classifyTriangle(3, 3, 3)` returns `"equilateral"`, `classifyTriangle(1, 1, 5)` returns `"invalid"`.
hints: Handle validation first — if the sides are not valid, return early before trying to classify.
Check validity with `a <= 0 || b <= 0 || c <= 0 || a + b <= c || a + c <= b || b + c <= a`. Then use equality checks for classification.

exercises.title: Nested If
exercises.description: Calculate pay with overtime and weekend multiplier rules.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `calculatePay` that takes `hours`, `rate`, and a boolean `isWeekend`.

Pay rules:
- First 40 hours are paid at the regular `rate`
- Hours over 40 are paid at 1.5x the regular `rate` (overtime)
- If `isWeekend` is `true`, multiply the total pay by 1.5

Example: `calculatePay(50, 20, false)` returns `1100` (800 regular + 300 overtime).
`calculatePay(50, 20, true)` returns `1650` (1100 * 1.5 weekend).
hints: Break the problem into two parts: first calculate base pay with possible overtime, then apply the weekend multiplier if needed.
Calculate regular pay for up to 40 hours, add overtime pay for hours beyond 40 at 1.5x, then multiply by 1.5 if isWeekend is true.

exercises.title: Complex If
exercises.description: Calculate shipping cost from weight brackets and zone multipliers.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getShippingRate` that takes a `weight` (in pounds) and a `zone` string.

Base rate by weight:
- Under 5 lbs: `$5`
- 5 to 20 lbs: `$10`
- Over 20 lbs: `$20`

Zone multiplier:
- `"local"`: 1x
- `"domestic"`: 2x
- `"international"`: 5x

Return the base rate multiplied by the zone multiplier.

Example: `getShippingRate(3, "domestic")` returns `10` ($5 base * 2x domestic).
hints: Solve one dimension at a time: first determine the base rate from weight, then apply the zone multiplier.
Use if/else-if/else to set a base rate variable, then use another if/else chain to multiply by the zone factor.

exercises.title: Complex If
exercises.description: Check multiple ride eligibility criteria and return specific failure reasons.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `canRide` that takes `height` (inches), `age`, and a boolean `hasHeartCondition`.

Check eligibility in this order:
1. If `hasHeartCondition` is true → return `"health restriction"`
2. If `height` is less than 48 → return `"too short"`
3. If `age` is less than 8 → return `"too young"`
4. If all checks pass → return `"approved"`

Example: `canRide(52, 10, false)` returns `"approved"`, `canRide(45, 10, false)` returns `"too short"`.
hints: Check each criterion one at a time and return immediately if it fails. The order matters — check the most critical restriction first.
Use separate `if` statements with early returns. If none of the failure conditions trigger, return "approved" at the end.

exercises.title: Conditionals: Combined
exercises.description: Combine switch, ternary, and if/else to rate a service.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `rateService` that takes a `serviceType` string, a `score` (1-10), and a boolean `isPremium`.

**Step 1 — Switch:** Map `serviceType` to a label:
- `"delivery"` → `"Delivery"`
- `"support"` → `"Support"`
- `"quality"` → `"Quality"`
- Anything else → `"General"`

**Step 2 — Ternary:** If `isPremium` is true, add 2 to the score. Otherwise, keep the score as-is.

**Step 3 — If/Else:** Classify the adjusted score:
- 8 or above → `"Excellent"`
- 5-7 → `"Good"`
- Below 5 → `"Needs Improvement"`

Return the label and classification joined with `": "`.

Example: `rateService("delivery", 9, false)` returns `"Delivery: Excellent"`.
`rateService("delivery", 6, true)` returns `"Delivery: Excellent"` (6 + 2 = 8).
hints: Break the problem into three distinct steps. Solve each one independently using the appropriate conditional tool.
Use `switch` to set a label variable, a ternary to calculate the adjusted score, and `if/else` to set a rating variable. Combine them at the end.

exercises.title: String: Length and Access
exercises.description: Return the last character of a string using .length and bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
Strings have a `.length` property that tells you how many characters they contain. You can access individual characters using bracket notation `str[index]` or the `.charAt(index)` method. Indices start at 0.

Write a function called `getLastChar` that takes a string and returns its last character.

The last character is at index `str.length - 1`.

Example: `getLastChar("hello")` returns `"o"`, `getLastChar("a")` returns `"a"`.
hints: The `.length` property gives the total number of characters. Since indices start at 0, the last character is one less than the length.
Access the last character with `str[str.length - 1]`.

exercises.title: String: toLowerCase
exercises.description: Normalize an email address to lowercase and trimmed.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `normalizeEmail` that takes an email string and returns it lowercased with whitespace trimmed from both sides.

Use `.toLowerCase()` and `.trim()`.

Example: `normalizeEmail("  User@Email.COM  ")` returns `"user@email.com"`.
hints: You can chain string methods — the result of one method becomes the input to the next.
Call `.toLowerCase()` to convert all characters, then `.trim()` to remove whitespace from both ends.

exercises.title: String: toUpperCase
exercises.description: Convert a message to all uppercase letters.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `shoutMessage` that takes a string and returns it in all uppercase.

Example: `shoutMessage("hello world")` returns `"HELLO WORLD"`.
hints: The `.toUpperCase()` method returns a new string with all letters converted to uppercase. Numbers and symbols are unaffected.
Call `.toUpperCase()` on the message and return the result.

exercises.title: String: trim
exercises.description: Clean user input by trimming whitespace from both sides.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `cleanInput` that takes a string and returns it with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

Example: `cleanInput("  hello  ")` returns `"hello"`.
hints: The `.trim()` method removes whitespace from the beginning and end of a string, but not from the middle.
Call `.trim()` on the string and return the result.

exercises.title: String: trimStart
exercises.description: Remove only leading whitespace from a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `trimLeading` that takes a string and returns it with only the leading (left-side) whitespace removed. Trailing whitespace should remain.

Example: `trimLeading("  hello  ")` returns `"hello  "`.
hints: `.trimStart()` only removes whitespace from the beginning of the string, leaving the end untouched.
Call `.trimStart()` on the string and return the result.

exercises.title: String: trimEnd
exercises.description: Remove only trailing whitespace from a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `trimTrailing` that takes a string and returns it with only the trailing (right-side) whitespace removed. Leading whitespace should remain.

Example: `trimTrailing("  hello  ")` returns `"  hello"`.
hints: `.trimEnd()` only removes whitespace from the end of the string, leaving the beginning untouched.
Call `.trimEnd()` on the string and return the result.

exercises.title: String: includes
exercises.description: Check if a string contains a target word.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `containsWord` that takes a `text` string and a `word` string. Return `true` if the text contains the word, `false` otherwise.

Use `.includes()` which returns a boolean.

Example: `containsWord("hello world", "world")` returns `true`.
hints: `.includes()` checks if a string contains another string and returns `true` or `false`. It is case-sensitive.
Call `.includes()` on the text with the word as the argument and return the result.

exercises.title: String: startsWith
exercises.description: Check if a URL starts with the HTTPS protocol.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isHttps` that takes a `url` string and returns `true` if it starts with `"https://"`, `false` otherwise.

Example: `isHttps("https://example.com")` returns `true`, `isHttps("http://example.com")` returns `false`.
hints: `.startsWith()` checks if a string begins with a specific sequence of characters. It is case-sensitive.
Call `.startsWith("https://")` on the url and return the result.

exercises.title: String: endsWith
exercises.description: Check if a filename ends with a given file extension.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `hasExtension` that takes a `filename` and an `ext` string (like `".js"`, `".html"`). Return `true` if the filename ends with that extension, `false` otherwise.

Example: `hasExtension("app.js", ".js")` returns `true`, `hasExtension("style.css", ".js")` returns `false`.
hints: `.endsWith()` checks if a string ends with a specific sequence of characters. It is case-sensitive.
Call `.endsWith()` on the filename with the extension as the argument.

exercises.title: String: indexOf
exercises.description: Find the first position of a character in a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `findCharPosition` that takes a `str` and a `char`. Return the index of the first occurrence of `char` in `str`, or `-1` if not found.

`.indexOf()` returns the position (starting at 0) of the first match, or `-1` if no match exists.

Example: `findCharPosition("hello", "l")` returns `2`, `findCharPosition("hello", "z")` returns `-1`.
hints: `.indexOf()` searches from the beginning and returns the position of the first match. Positions start at 0.
Call `.indexOf()` on the string with the character as the argument and return the result.

exercises.title: String: lastIndexOf
exercises.description: Find the last position of a character in a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `findLastOccurrence` that takes a `str` and a `char`. Return the index of the last occurrence of `char` in `str`, or `-1` if not found.

`.lastIndexOf()` searches from the end of the string backward.

Example: `findLastOccurrence("banana", "a")` returns `5`, `findLastOccurrence("hello", "z")` returns `-1`.
hints: `.lastIndexOf()` works like `.indexOf()` but searches backward from the end of the string.
Call `.lastIndexOf()` on the string with the character as the argument.

exercises.title: String: slice
exercises.description: Extract the first name from a full name string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getFirstName` that takes a `fullName` string in the format `"First Last"` and returns just the first name.

Use `.indexOf(" ")` to find the space, then `.slice(0, spaceIndex)` to extract everything before it.

Example: `getFirstName("John Smith")` returns `"John"`.
hints: First find where the space is using `.indexOf(" ")`, then extract from the start up to that position.
Use `.slice(0, spaceIndex)` where `spaceIndex` comes from `.indexOf(" ")`. You can chain or use a variable.

exercises.title: String: slice
exercises.description: Extract the file extension from a filename using negative slice.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `getExtension` that takes a `filename` string and returns the file extension including the dot.

Use `.lastIndexOf(".")` to find the dot, then `.slice()` from that position to the end.

Example: `getExtension("app.js")` returns `".js"`, `getExtension("photo.png")` returns `".png"`.
hints: `.lastIndexOf(".")` finds the position of the last dot. `.slice()` from that position extracts everything from the dot onward.
Call `.slice(dotIndex)` where `dotIndex` is `filename.lastIndexOf(".")`. When `.slice()` gets one argument, it extracts to the end.

exercises.title: String: replace
exercises.description: Replace the first occurrence of a word with asterisks.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `censor` that takes a `text` string and a `word` to censor. Replace the first occurrence of the word with asterisks (`*`) of the same length.

Use `.repeat()` to build the asterisk string and `.replace()` to swap it in.

Example: `censor("oh snap that was bad", "snap")` returns `"oh **** that was bad"`.
hints: `.replace()` swaps the first match with a replacement string. `.repeat(n)` creates a string of a character repeated n times.
Build the replacement with `"*".repeat(word.length)` then pass both to `.replace()`.

exercises.title: String: replaceAll
exercises.description: Replace ALL occurrences of a word with asterisks.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `censorAll` that takes a `text` string and a `word` to censor. Replace every occurrence of the word with asterisks of matching length.

`.replaceAll()` replaces all matches, unlike `.replace()` which only replaces the first.

Example: `censorAll("ha ha ha", "ha")` returns `"** ** **"`.
hints: `.replaceAll()` works like `.replace()` but swaps every occurrence, not just the first.
Use `.replaceAll(word, "*".repeat(word.length))` to replace every match with the right number of asterisks.

exercises.title: String: repeat
exercises.description: Build a separator line of repeated characters.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `buildSeparator` that takes a `char` and a `count`. Return a string of that character repeated `count` times.

Example: `buildSeparator("-", 10)` returns `"----------"`, `buildSeparator("=", 5)` returns `"====="`.
hints: `.repeat(n)` creates a new string by repeating the original string n times.
Call `.repeat()` on the character with the count as the argument.

exercises.title: String: padStart
exercises.description: Pad a number string with leading zeros to a fixed width.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `padNumber` that takes a `numStr` (number as a string) and a `width`. Return the string padded with leading zeros so it is at least `width` characters long.

Example: `padNumber("42", 5)` returns `"00042"`, `padNumber("123", 3)` returns `"123"`.
hints: `.padStart(targetLength, padString)` adds characters to the beginning of a string until it reaches the target length.
Call `.padStart(width, "0")` on the number string to fill with leading zeros.

exercises.title: String: padEnd
exercises.description: Pad a label with trailing dots to a fixed width.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `padLabel` that takes a `label` string and a `width`. Return the label padded with trailing dots (`.`) so it is at least `width` characters long.

Example: `padLabel("Name", 10)` returns `"Name......"`, `padLabel("Price", 5)` returns `"Price"`.
hints: `.padEnd(targetLength, padString)` adds characters to the end of a string until it reaches the target length.
Call `.padEnd(width, ".")` on the label to fill with trailing dots.

exercises.title: String: split
exercises.description: Split a string by spaces and return the word count.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countWords` that takes a `text` string and returns the number of words. Words are separated by spaces.

`.split(separator)` divides a string into an array. Use `.length` on the result to count.

Example: `countWords("hello world")` returns `2`, `countWords("one")` returns `1`.
hints: `.split()` divides a string into an array using the separator you provide. The array has a `.length` property.
Call `.split(" ")` to get an array of words, then access `.length` to count them.

exercises.title: String Methods: Combined
exercises.description: Format a 10-digit string as a phone number using concatenation and slice.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `formatPhone` that takes a 10-digit string and returns it formatted as `(###) ###-####`.

Use string concatenation and `.slice()` to extract the area code, prefix, and line number.

Example: `formatPhone("5551234567")` returns `"(555) 123-4567"`.
hints: Break the 10 digits into three groups: first 3 (area code), next 3 (prefix), last 4 (line number). Use `.slice()` for each group.
Use `.slice(0, 3)` for area code, `.slice(3, 6)` for prefix, `.slice(6)` for the rest. Concatenate with parentheses, space, and dash.

exercises.title: reverseString
exercises.description: Reverse a string character by character using a loop.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `reverseString` that takes a string and returns it reversed.

Use a `for` loop that iterates through the string from the last character to the first, building a new string.

Example: `reverseString("hello")` returns `"olleh"`, `reverseString("abc")` returns `"cba"`.
hints: Start with an empty result string and loop through the original string backward, appending each character.
Loop from `str.length - 1` down to `0`, adding `str[i]` to the result on each iteration.

exercises.title: isPalindrome
exercises.description: Check if a string reads the same forwards and backwards.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `isPalindrome` that takes a string and returns `true` if it reads the same forwards and backwards (case-insensitive), `false` otherwise.

Convert to lowercase first, then compare characters from each end moving inward.

Example: `isPalindrome("racecar")` returns `true`, `isPalindrome("hello")` returns `false`, `isPalindrome("Madam")` returns `true`.
hints: First convert to lowercase so the comparison is case-insensitive. Then compare characters from opposite ends of the string.
Use `.toLowerCase()` first. Loop from `0` to halfway, comparing `str[i]` with `str[str.length - 1 - i]`. If any pair differs, return false.

exercises.title: countVowels
exercises.description: Count the number of vowels in a string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countVowels` that takes a string and returns the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) it contains. The check should be case-insensitive.

Example: `countVowels("hello")` returns `2`, `countVowels("rhythm")` returns `0`.
hints: Convert to lowercase first so the check works for both cases. Loop through each character and check if it is a vowel.
Use `.toLowerCase()` then loop through each character. Check `"aeiou".includes(char)` to test if it is a vowel.

exercises.title: truncate
exercises.description: Truncate a string to a maximum length and append an ellipsis.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `truncate` that takes a `str` and a `maxLength`. If the string is longer than `maxLength`, return the first `maxLength` characters followed by `"..."`. Otherwise, return the string unchanged.

Example: `truncate("Hello World", 5)` returns `"Hello..."`, `truncate("Hi", 10)` returns `"Hi"`.
hints: Check if the string is longer than the maximum. If so, use `.slice()` to take the first `maxLength` characters and add `"..."`.
Compare `str.length > maxLength`. If true, return `str.slice(0, maxLength) + "..."`. Otherwise return `str` as-is.

exercises.title: maskCardString
exercises.description: Mask all but the last 4 digits of a credit card string with asterisks.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `maskCardString` that takes a credit card number as a string and returns it with all but the last 4 characters replaced by asterisks.

Use `.slice()` to get the last 4 characters, and `"*".repeat()` to build the mask.

Example: `maskCardString("4111111111111111")` returns `"************1111"`.
hints: Use `.slice(-4)` to grab the last 4 characters. Then build the asterisk mask using `.repeat()` with the right count.
Get the last 4 with `cardStr.slice(-4)`. Build the mask with `"*".repeat(cardStr.length - 4)`. Concatenate mask + last four.

exercises.title: Array: Nested Access
exercises.description: Return an element from a two-dimensional array using chained bracket notation.
exercises.instructions:
Arrays can contain other arrays, creating a two-dimensional grid (often called a matrix). To access an element, chain bracket notation: `matrix[row][col]`.

Write a function called `getCell` that takes a 2D array, a row index, and a column index, and returns the element at that position.

Example: `getCell([[1,2],[3,4]], 1, 0)` returns `3`.
hints: A 2D array is just an array of arrays. The first bracket selects which inner array (row), and the second bracket selects the element within that row.
Chain two bracket accesses together: `matrix[row][col]` — the first picks the row, the second picks the column.

exercises.title: Array: Deep Access
exercises.description: Navigate three levels of nested arrays to retrieve a deeply nested value.
exercises.instructions:
When arrays are nested three or more levels deep, you chain additional brackets to reach the target. Each bracket digs one level deeper.

Write a function called `getDeepValue` that takes a 3D array and three indices (`i`, `j`, `k`), and returns `data[i][j][k]`.

Example: `getDeepValue([[[1,2],[3,4]],[[5,6],[7,8]]], 1, 0, 1)` returns `6`.
hints: Each pair of brackets accesses one level deeper. With three levels of nesting, you need three pairs of brackets chained together.
Access the value step by step: `data[i]` gets the outer array, `data[i][j]` gets the middle array, and `data[i][j][k]` gets the final value.

exercises.title: Array: Length and Last
exercises.description: Use the .length property to dynamically access the last element of an array.
exercises.instructions:
Every array has a `.length` property that tells you how many elements it contains. Since array indices start at 0, the last element is always at index `arr.length - 1`.

Write a function called `getLastElement` that takes an array and returns its last element without hardcoding the index.

Example: `getLastElement([10, 20, 30])` returns `30`.
hints: The `.length` property gives you the total count of elements. Since indices start at 0, the last index is always one less than the length.
Access the last element with `arr[arr.length - 1]` — this works for any array size.

exercises.title: Array: push
exercises.description: Add elements to the end of an array using the .push() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.push()` method adds one or more elements to the end of an array and returns the new length. It mutates (changes) the original array.

Write a function called `addToEnd` that takes an array and an item, pushes the item onto the array, and returns the updated array.

Example: `addToEnd([1, 2], 3)` returns `[1, 2, 3]`.
hints: The `.push()` method adds an element to the end of the array. Remember that it changes the original array in place.
Call `arr.push(item)` to add the item, then return `arr` — push modifies the array but returns the new length, not the array.

exercises.title: Array: pop
exercises.description: Remove the last element from an array using the .pop() method and return it.
exercises.instructions:
The `.pop()` method removes the last element from an array and returns that removed element. It mutates the original array.

Write a function called `removeFromEnd` that takes an array, removes the last element, and returns an object with `removed` (the removed element) and `array` (the updated array).

Example: `removeFromEnd([1, 2, 3])` returns `{ removed: 3, array: [1, 2] }`.
hints: The `.pop()` method removes and returns the last element. Save its return value to a variable before returning your result.
Call `const removed = arr.pop()` to capture the removed element, then return an object with both `removed` and `array`.

exercises.title: Array: push and pop
exercises.description: Combine push and pop to rotate elements through a fixed-size queue.
exercises.instructions:
When push and pop are used together, you can create a fixed-size queue: remove the oldest element (pop from front would use shift, but here we pop from end) and add a new one.

Write a function called `rotatePush` that takes an array and a new item. It should remove the first element using a combination of techniques, push the new item to the end, and return an object with `removed` (the old first element) and `array` (the updated array).

Hint: You can remove the first element by saving it, then rebuilding with slice and push, or use shift.

Example: `rotatePush([1, 2, 3], 4)` returns `{ removed: 1, array: [2, 3, 4] }`.
hints: Think about which method removes from the front (shift) and which adds to the end (push). Combine them to rotate elements through the array.
Use `arr.shift()` to remove the first element, then `arr.push(newItem)` to add the new one at the end.

exercises.title: Array: unshift
exercises.description: Add elements to the beginning of an array using the .unshift() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.unshift()` method adds one or more elements to the beginning of an array and returns the new length. It mutates the original array.

Write a function called `addToFront` that takes an array and an item, adds the item to the front, and returns the updated array.

Example: `addToFront([2, 3], 1)` returns `[1, 2, 3]`.
hints: The `.unshift()` method is like `.push()` but adds to the beginning instead of the end. It also mutates the original array.
Call `arr.unshift(item)` to add the item to the front, then return `arr` — unshift returns the new length, not the array.

exercises.title: Array: shift
exercises.description: Remove the first element from an array using the .shift() method and return it.
exercises.instructions:
The `.shift()` method removes the first element from an array and returns that removed element. It mutates the original array.

Write a function called `removeFromFront` that takes an array, removes the first element, and returns an object with `removed` (the removed element) and `array` (the updated array).

Example: `removeFromFront([1, 2, 3])` returns `{ removed: 1, array: [2, 3] }`.
hints: The `.shift()` method is like `.pop()` but removes from the beginning instead of the end. Save its return value before building your result.
Call `const removed = arr.shift()` to capture the removed element, then return an object with both `removed` and `array`.

exercises.title: Array: shift and unshift
exercises.description: Combine shift and unshift to cycle array elements forward by one position.
exercises.instructions:
By combining shift and unshift, you can rotate elements in an array. Shifting removes from the front, and unshifting adds to the front.

Write a function called `cycleForward` that takes an array, removes the last element, and inserts it at the beginning — cycling all elements forward by one position.

Example: `cycleForward([1, 2, 3, 4])` returns `[4, 1, 2, 3]`.
hints: To cycle forward, you need to take the last element and put it at the beginning. Think about which method removes from the end and which adds to the beginning.
Use `arr.pop()` to grab the last element, then `arr.unshift(last)` to put it at the front.

exercises.title: Array: includes
exercises.description: Check whether an array contains a specific value using the .includes() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.includes()` method checks if an array contains a certain value and returns `true` or `false`. It uses strict equality (`===`) for comparison.

Write a function called `hasItem` that takes an array and a target value, and returns whether the array contains that value.

Example: `hasItem([1, 2, 3], 2)` returns `true`, `hasItem([1, 2, 3], 5)` returns `false`.
hints: The `.includes()` method returns a boolean — `true` if the value is found, `false` otherwise. No loops or conditionals needed.
Simply return the result of `arr.includes(target)` directly — it already gives you a boolean.

exercises.title: Array: indexOf
exercises.description: Find the first position of a value in an array using the .indexOf() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.indexOf()` method returns the first index at which a value is found, or `-1` if the value is not in the array. It searches from left to right.

Write a function called `findFirstPosition` that takes an array and a target, and returns the index of the first occurrence. Return `-1` if not found.

Example: `findFirstPosition([10, 20, 30, 20], 20)` returns `1`.
hints: The `.indexOf()` method searches from left to right and returns the position of the first match. If no match is found, it returns -1.
Return the result of `arr.indexOf(target)` directly — it handles both the found and not-found cases.

exercises.title: Array: lastIndexOf
exercises.description: Find the last position of a value in an array using the .lastIndexOf() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.lastIndexOf()` method returns the last index at which a value is found, or `-1` if not present. It searches from right to left.

Write a function called `findLastPosition` that takes an array and a target, and returns the index of the last occurrence.

Example: `findLastPosition([10, 20, 30, 20], 20)` returns `3`.
hints: The `.lastIndexOf()` method works like `.indexOf()` but searches from right to left, returning the position of the last match.
Return `arr.lastIndexOf(target)` directly — it gives -1 when not found, just like indexOf.

exercises.title: Array: Search Combined
exercises.description: Use indexOf in a loop to find all positions of a value in an array.
exercises.instructions:
Neither `.indexOf()` nor `.lastIndexOf()` return all positions of a value. To find every occurrence, use `.indexOf()` in a loop with a starting index.

`.indexOf(target, fromIndex)` accepts an optional second argument that tells it where to start searching.

Write a function called `findAllPositions` that takes an array and a target, and returns an array of all indices where the target appears. Return an empty array if not found.

Example: `findAllPositions([1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2], 2)` returns `[1, 3, 5]`.
hints: Use `.indexOf(target, fromIndex)` where `fromIndex` starts after the last found position. Keep searching until indexOf returns -1.
Start with `let index = arr.indexOf(target)`. In a while loop, push the index to your results array, then search again from `index + 1`.

exercises.title: Array: slice
exercises.description: Extract a portion of an array without changing the original using .slice().
exercises.instructions:
The `.slice(start, end)` method returns a shallow copy of a portion of an array. It does NOT mutate the original. The `start` index is included, and the `end` index is excluded.

Write a function called `getSubArray` that takes an array, a start index, and an end index, and returns the extracted portion.

Example: `getSubArray([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], 1, 4)` returns `[20, 30, 40]`.
hints: Think of `.slice(start, end)` as "from here, up to but not including there." The original array stays untouched.
Return `arr.slice(start, end)` directly — it creates and returns a new array with the extracted elements.

exercises.title: Array: splice
exercises.description: Insert an element at a specific position in an array using .splice().
exercises.instructions:
The `.splice(index, deleteCount, ...items)` method changes an array by removing, replacing, or adding elements at a specific position. It mutates the original array.

Write a function called `insertAtIndex` that takes an array, an index, and an item. It should insert the item at that index without removing anything, and return the updated array.

Example: `insertAtIndex([1, 2, 4, 5], 2, 3)` returns `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.
hints: The `.splice()` method takes three arguments here: the position to insert at, how many elements to remove (0 for pure insert), and the new element.
Call `arr.splice(index, 0, item)` — the 0 means "delete nothing, just insert." Then return the modified array.

exercises.title: Array: concat
exercises.description: Combine two arrays into a new array using the .concat() method.
exercises.instructions:
The `.concat()` method merges two or more arrays into a new array. It does NOT mutate the originals.

Write a function called `mergeArrays` that takes two arrays and returns a new array containing all elements from both, with the first array's elements appearing first.

Example: `mergeArrays([1, 2], [3, 4])` returns `[1, 2, 3, 4]`.
hints: The `.concat()` method returns a brand new array without changing either original. Think of it as gluing two arrays end-to-end.
Return `arr1.concat(arr2)` directly — it creates a new array with arr1's elements followed by arr2's elements.

exercises.title: Array: reverse
exercises.description: Reverse an array without mutating the original using slice and reverse.
exercises.instructions:
The `.reverse()` method reverses an array in place — but what if you need to keep the original intact? By combining `.slice()` (to make a copy) with `.reverse()`, you can reverse without mutation.

Write a function called `reverseArray` that takes an array and returns a new reversed array without changing the original.

Example: `reverseArray([1, 2, 3])` returns `[3, 2, 1]`.
hints: The `.reverse()` method mutates the original array. To avoid this, make a copy first. `.slice()` with no arguments returns a full copy.
Chain `.slice().reverse()` — slice creates the copy, then reverse works on the copy instead of the original.

exercises.title: Array: join
exercises.description: Join array elements into a formatted string with commas and "and" before the last item.
exercises.instructions:
The `.join(separator)` method combines all elements of an array into a single string, with the separator between each element.

Write a function called `formatList` that takes an array of strings and returns a natural-language list. If there's one item, return it. If there are two, join with " and ". If three or more, join all but the last with ", " and add " and " before the last item.

Examples:
- `formatList(["apple"])` returns `"apple"`
- `formatList(["apple", "banana"])` returns `"apple and banana"`
- `formatList(["apple", "banana", "cherry"])` returns `"apple, banana and cherry"`
hints: Handle the three cases separately: one item (return it), two items (join with " and "), and three or more (join all but last with ", " then add " and " + last).
For 3+ items, use `items.slice(0, -1).join(", ")` to get everything except the last item as a comma string, then concatenate `" and " + items[items.length - 1]`.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Basics
exercises.description: Generate all coordinate strings for a grid using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely for each iteration of the outer loop. This lets you work with combinations, grids, and multi-dimensional data.

Write a function called `gridCoordinates` that takes `rows` and `cols` (both numbers) and returns an array of coordinate strings in the format `"(row,col)"`. Iterate through every row and column combination.

Example: `gridCoordinates(2, 3)` returns `["(0,0)", "(0,1)", "(0,2)", "(1,0)", "(1,1)", "(1,2)"]`.
hints: A nested loop has an outer loop and an inner loop. The inner loop runs all its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop. For a 2×3 grid, the inner loop runs 3 times for row 0, then 3 times for row 1.
Use two `for` loops — the outer with `i < rows`, the inner with `j < cols`. Inside the inner loop, push `"(" + i + "," + j + ")"` to your results array.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Pairs
exercises.description: Return all unique pairs from an array using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `uniquePairs` that takes an array and returns all unique pairs as an array of two-element arrays. Each pair should be `[arr[i], arr[j]]` where `j` is always greater than `i` — this avoids duplicate pairs and self-pairing.

Example: `uniquePairs(["a", "b", "c"])` returns `[["a","b"], ["a","c"], ["b","c"]]`.

Example: `uniquePairs([1, 2, 3, 4])` returns `[[1,2], [1,3], [1,4], [2,3], [2,4], [3,4]]`.
hints: The key is making the inner loop start at `i + 1` instead of 0. This ensures you only pair each element with the elements that come after it, avoiding duplicates and self-pairs.
Outer loop: `for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++)`. Inner loop: `for (let j = i + 1; j < arr.length; j++)`. Push `[arr[i], arr[j]]` each time.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Find First
exercises.description: Search a 2D array for the first occurrence of a target value.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `findIn2D` that takes a `grid` (an array of arrays) and a `target` value. Search through the grid row by row, column by column, and return `[row, col]` for the first occurrence of the target. If the target is not found, return `[-1, -1]`.

Example: `findIn2D([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]], 4)` returns `[1, 1]`.

Example: `findIn2D([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 99)` returns `[-1, -1]`.
hints: Use nested loops to visit every cell: outer loop for rows (`i`), inner loop for columns (`j`). Check each cell with `grid[i][j] === target`.
When you find the target, `return [i, j]` immediately — this exits both loops. If the loops finish without finding it, `return [-1, -1]` after the outer loop.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Find All
exercises.description: Search a 2D array and return the positions of all occurrences of a target value.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `findAllIn2D` that takes a `grid` (an array of arrays) and a `target` value. Search through every cell and return an array of `[row, col]` pairs for ALL occurrences. If the target is not found, return an empty array.

Example: `findAllIn2D([[1, 2, 1], [3, 1, 4]], 1)` returns `[[0, 0], [0, 2], [1, 1]]`.

Example: `findAllIn2D([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 5)` returns `[]`.
hints: Unlike Find First, do NOT return early when you find a match. Instead, push each `[i, j]` match into a results array and keep going through the entire grid.
Create an empty results array before the loops. Inside the inner loop, use `if (grid[i][j] === target)` to push `[i, j]`. After both loops finish, return the results array.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Triangle
exercises.description: Build a right triangle pattern of stars as a multi-line string using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `buildTriangle` that takes a number `n` and returns a right triangle of `*` characters as a single string. Row 1 has 1 star, row 2 has 2 stars, and so on up to `n` stars. Separate each row with `\n` (a newline character). Do not add a trailing newline.

Example: `buildTriangle(3)` returns `"*\n**\n***"` which displays as:

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Reverse Triangle
exercises.description: Build a right-aligned triangle of stars with leading spaces as a multi-line string.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `buildReverseTriangle` that takes a number `n` and returns a right-aligned triangle of `*` characters as a single string. Row 1 has `n - 1` leading spaces and 1 star, row 2 has `n - 2` spaces and 2 stars, continuing until the last row has 0 spaces and `n` stars. Separate each row with `\n`. exercises.title: Nested Loops: Flatten
exercises.description: Flatten a 2D array into a 1D array using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `flatten2D` that takes a `grid` (an array of arrays) and returns a single flat array containing all elements in row-major order. Use nested loops — do not use `.flat()`, `.concat()`, or spread syntax.

Example: `flatten2D([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]])` returns `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.

Example: `flatten2D([["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]])` returns `["a", "b", "c", "d"]`.
hints: Use the outer loop to iterate over each inner array (row), and the inner loop to iterate over each element within that row. Push each element into a results array.
Outer loop: `for (let i = 0; i < grid.length; i++)`. Inner loop: `for (let j = 0; j < grid[i].length; j++)`. Push `grid[i][j]` to the result array each time.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Multiplication Table
exercises.description: Build a 2D multiplication table using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `multiplicationTable` that takes a number `n` and returns a 2D array representing an n×n multiplication table. Each cell at `[i][j]` should contain `(i + 1) * (j + 1)`. The outer array represents rows, and each inner array represents a row of products.

Example: `multiplicationTable(3)` returns `[[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [3, 6, 9]]`.

Example: `multiplicationTable(1)` returns `[[1]]`.
hints: This is the inverse of flattening — you are building a 2D array. The outer loop creates each row, and the inner loop fills that row with products.
Create an empty `table` array. Outer loop: create a new `row` array, inner loop: push `(i + 1) * (j + 1)` into the row. After the inner loop, push the completed row into the table.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Common Elements
exercises.description: Find elements that appear in both arrays using nested loops.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `commonElements` that takes two arrays and returns a new array containing only the elements that appear in both. Use nested loops to compare — do not use `.includes()`, `.indexOf()`, or Set. Assume neither input array contains duplicate values.

Example: `commonElements([1, 2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5, 6])` returns `[3, 4]`.

Example: `commonElements([1, 2], [3, 4])` returns `[]`.
hints: For each element in the first array, loop through the entire second array looking for a match. If you find one, add it to the result and `break` out of the inner loop.
Outer loop over `arr1`, inner loop over `arr2`. When `arr1[i] === arr2[j]`, push `arr1[i]` to results and `break`. The `break` stops the inner loop since you already found the match.

exercises.title: Nested Loops: Pyramid
exercises.description: Build a centered pyramid of stars as a multi-line string using nested loops.

Write a function called `buildPyramid` that takes a number `n` and returns a centered pyramid of `*` characters as a single string. Each row has leading spaces to center the stars. Row 1 has 1 star, row 2 has 3 stars, row 3 has 5 stars, and so on (increasing by 2). Separate rows with `\n`. Do not add a trailing newline.

For each row `i` (starting at 0): spaces = `n - i - 1`, stars = `2 * i + 1`.

Example: `buildPyramid(3)` returns `"  *\n ***\n*****"` which displays as:
```
  *
 ***
*****
```

Example: `buildPyramid(1)` returns `"*"`.
